# hack-n-learn

> Notes by Srikanth Venugopalan on building a distributed, petabyte-scale analytical query engine, and on the architecture around it: query execution, indexing, vector search, lakehouse storage (Apache Iceberg, Parquet), distributed and multi-cloud execution, and what data systems need as AI agents become their users. Also notes from 2017 to 2025 on Gauge, the open-source test automation framework: wire protocols, plugin supervision, loading user code in .NET, telemetry, and keeping a project alive after its sponsor stepped back.

The author works on OLAP query engines at e6data. Each note is written from first-hand engineering work and dated to when the work happened. Earlier writing (2012 to 2013) is also on the site.

Every note is available as plain markdown by replacing the trailing slash of its URL with `.md`, and all of them together at https://sriv.github.io/llms-full.txt.


---

# From one terabyte to ten

By Srikanth Venugopalan, 16 October 2026. Topics: distributed.
Canonical: https://sriv.github.io/notes/from-one-terabyte-to-ten/

> A distributed query engine that works at one terabyte has proved very little about ten. The lessons from this autumn, minus the numbers.

This autumn I went back to distributed execution, this time on the Rust engine, with a simple-sounding goal: take a set of analytical queries that run well on one big machine and make them complete and stay fast when the data grows tenfold and the work spreads across many machines.

I'm not going to share numbers here. But the lessons don't need them, and most of them are things I wish someone had told me at the start.

## Write the goals down, and make them per query

The first useful thing we did was agree on what "working" means, in writing, before any more runs:

- **Every query completes.** Not most of them. A query that fails at ten terabytes is a bug, not a statistic.
- **No query gets slower because distribution exists.** That applies to queries that distribute *and* to queries that don't. On a cluster of smaller machines, a query that stays on one node is running on a fraction of the hardware it had before, so "leave it alone" isn't neutral. It's a regression.
- **Never change the single-node plan to help the distributed one.** Anything that only matters when distributing has to be decided inside the distributed path.

The second rule is the one that changed how we looked at results. A total runtime can improve while a dozen individual queries get several times slower. Totals are for slides. Per-query comparisons against a single-node baseline are for engineering.

## The coordinator is your serial fraction

The easy way to distribute a single-node engine is to split the scans across workers and pull everything above them back to one coordinating node. It works well at first, because scans are where most of the time goes on small data.

It stops working as the data grows, and Amdahl's law tells you exactly why. Whatever still runs on the coordinator (joins, final aggregations, window functions, anything over a materialised intermediate result) is the serial part of the job. Add machines and the parallel part shrinks, but the coordinator's time doesn't, so its share grows until it is most of the runtime. And when that work grows with the input, ten times the data makes the serial part ten times bigger as well.

The measure that taught me the most was simply: **what fraction of each query's time is spent on the coordinator?** A rule I'd now give any team: coordinator work should be proportional to the size of the *result*, not the size of the *input*. Any operator that breaks that rule doesn't belong on the coordinator. It's next on the list to distribute.

[Diagram: Query time split into work spread across workers and work on the coordinator, for one, two, four and eight workers. The spread part halves each time the workers double; the coordinator part stays the same length, so it becomes most of the runtime.]

*Amdahl's law with a name on it. Add machines and the coordinator's share is what's left.*

## Spill is not a distribution strategy

When queries run out of memory at ten terabytes, turning on spill-to-disk is tempting. It looks like it should make the failures go away. When we tried it across the whole query set, the result was worse, not better: more queries failed rather than fewer, and some that used to be fast got several times slower.

The better answer is almost always to spread the working set. A large intermediate result that doesn't fit on one machine often fits comfortably across four. Spill, and materialising intermediate results to storage, are last resorts for when there's genuinely nowhere left to put the data, not a substitute for distributing the work.

## Understand before you run

A full run at this scale ties up a fleet of large machines for a long time. Early on we fell into a loop: guess a cause, change something, run again, see no difference, guess again. After the third run in a row that didn't move anything, I started calling it rock, paper, scissors, and we stopped.

What replaced it:

- **Stop guessing and explain the slowdown from the data you already have.** Split each query's wall time into coordinator work, worker compute, time waiting on exchanges, and idle time. The answer was usually already sitting in the output of the last run.
- **One run per mechanism, with the prediction written first.** If you can't say what number should move and by roughly how much, you don't understand it yet.
- **Never change two things in one run.** We once changed a setting and the set of queries in the same run, and the result couldn't be compared to anything.

## Reproduce big problems on a small machine

Most of the debugging happened on a laptop, not in the cloud. The trick is that you don't need ten terabytes to reproduce a ten-terabyte failure. You need the same *pressure*. Run a smaller dataset across several local workers and squeeze each worker's memory until the same queries fail in the same places. The failure shapes carry over remarkably well.

Two cautions from doing this:

- **Collect statistics first.** Without table statistics, the planner falls back to heuristics, often little better than the order the query was written in, and you end up measuring the planner instead of the engine.
- **Keep a correctness oracle.** Every distributed run gets compared against a single-node run of the same queries, as unordered rows with a tolerance for floating point, of the same queries. A distributed engine that's fast and occasionally wrong is worse than useless.

## Bugs that need two machines

Some bugs don't exist until there's more than one node. Two kinds caught me out:

- **A reader that stops reading can block every writer.** An inner hash join with an empty build side can reasonably decide not to read its probe input at all, and a `LIMIT` that has seen enough rows can stop reading the rest. In one process that's a free shortcut. In a distributed plan, that input is often an exchange, and its writers on other machines sit waiting for reads that will never come. Every consumer of an exchange has to either drain it or say clearly that it's done.
- **Shared flow control hides in the transport.** Many logical streams multiplexed over one connection share that connection's flow-control window. If enough of them stall, all of them stall. That bug appeared only with two or more nodes and disappeared when buffers were made huge, which is exactly the pattern to look for.

The general lesson is to make hangs talk. A warning that says "this exchange has been stalled for five seconds, and here's who is waiting on whom" turns a frozen query into a bug report.

## A green run that didn't distribute

The most expensive mistake of the autumn wasn't in the engine. A missing setting meant the workers never registered as members of the cluster, so nothing distributed. Every query still ran on the coordinator and passed, slowly. We ran several large benchmarks before noticing that we'd been measuring a single-node engine on a multi-node bill.

In the same vein, a per-node agent added to every machine in the cluster quietly took up a little memory. That was enough for our executor's memory request to stop fitting, and the setup step reported it as a capacity problem.

Both teach the same lesson: **record the decision, not just the outcome.** Each query now records whether it distributed, how, and if not, why not. Each run checks that its machines are the ones it asked for. A result from a setup you haven't checked is just a number.

## Scale shows you which plans were only lucky

The last lesson is about the planner. At one terabyte, a few queries were planned badly and nobody noticed, because a bad plan over modest data still finishes. At ten terabytes the same plan never finishes. One query with join keys buried inside `OR` branches got a nested-loop join, which was a minor slowdown at small scale and impossible at large scale.

Scaling up is the most reliable bug-finder you have for the planner. Anything quadratic is waiting for you there.

## Where we're taking it

All of the above is ground any team will cover when they distribute a single-node engine, and none of it depends on how we do things at [e6data](https://www.e6data.com/). Workload management, deciding what runs where and alongside what, is the part we've deliberately kept as our own, and it's where we've taken a different road. That deserves its own write-up when it's ready.

## What I'd tell a team about to scale up

- **Agree on per-query goals before you run anything big.** Including the queries you don't distribute.
- **Track the coordinator's share.** It's the number that tells you whether adding machines can help.
- **Distribute before you spill.**
- **Explain, predict, then run.** One mechanism per run, with the expected result written down first.
- **Reproduce at small scale under memory pressure, with statistics and an oracle.**
- **Record every distribution decision, and check the setup of every run.** A run that passes without distributing will happen to you.

---

# Indexes in an analytical engine: how they work and when they pay

By Srikanth Venugopalan, 23 August 2026. Topics: indexes, iceberg.
Canonical: https://sriv.github.io/notes/skipping-indexes/

> In an engine that reads files from object storage, most indexes exist to rule data out; a few point straight at rows. How each kind works, when it pays, where Iceberg's Puffin files fit, and what building them taught me.

Say "index" to someone who grew up on OLTP databases and they picture a B-tree: a structure that takes a key and walks to the row. Analytical engines have indexes too, but in an engine that reads files from object storage, most of them are built for a different job. A query that aggregates millions of rows doesn't need a pointer to one of them. It needs to avoid reading the files and row groups that can't contribute. And when the data sits in object storage as immutable files, the cost that usually dominates is a request, not a row.

So the indexes in this note fall into two groups. Most are **skipping indexes**. They answer "which pieces of data can I prove don't contain what this query wants?", and say where a value can't be rather than where it is. A few, such as inverted and bitmap indexes, do point at rows: they hand the scan the exact positions worth decoding. Engines like Apache Druid, Apache Pinot and Apache Doris rely heavily on that second kind. Everything in [the cheapest row is the one you never read](https://sriv.github.io/notes/the-cheapest-row-is-the-one-you-never-read/) applies to both, including the one rule that matters most: an index may answer "maybe" as often as it likes, but it must never give a wrong "no".

I spent a good part of this year building a family of these indexes on Iceberg tables, from the writer that produces them to the reader that trusts them. This note is the general version: what each structure is, when it pays, where it lives, and the ways I've seen them go wrong.

## The ladder

An index works at some granularity, and the granularity decides both what it saves and what it costs.

[Diagram: The skipping ladder, from coarse to fine: partition (value-to-file maps, partition bounds), file (bounds in manifests, value sets, blooms), row group (Parquet statistics and blooms), page (Parquet page index), row (inverted index postings). Coarser levels are cheaper to ask, finer levels more precise. On object storage the file level saves the most.]

*Each level up is cheaper to ask and less precise.*

- **Partition.** Skip every file in a partition without opening any of them. Cheapest to consult, coarsest answer.
- **File.** Skip one data file. On object storage this is the one that matters most, because a skipped file means requests you never make.
- **Row group.** Skip a chunk inside a file you've already decided to open. Saves bytes and decoding, but you've paid for the footer.
- **Page.** Skip a single page inside a column chunk, typically up to a megabyte. Useful on selective queries over well-sorted data.
- **Row.** Hand the scan a bitmap of the rows worth reading. Precise, and the largest structures by far.

Every level up the ladder is cheaper to ask and less precise. The usual mistake is to build a fine-grained index when the expensive thing is coarse. If a query opens a thousand files to find matches in three, a row-level index inside each file doesn't fix it. You need something that rules out the other 997 before they're opened.

## The structures

### Min/max bounds

The oldest trick. For each column, keep the smallest and largest value in each file or row group. A predicate like `ts > '2026-08-01'` skips every chunk whose maximum is on or before that date.

Bounds are nearly free to compute and store, and Parquet and Iceberg both keep them already: Parquet per row group and, with the page index, per page; Iceberg per data file in its manifests. (Iceberg truncates string bounds and, by default, keeps them only for the first hundred columns.)

**When they pay:** when the data is sorted or clustered on the column, so each chunk covers a narrow range. Time columns in append-only tables are the classic case.

**When they don't:** when values are spread randomly across files. If every file's range is `a` to `z`, bounds rule out nothing. That's a layout problem, not an index problem, and the fix is sorting or clustering at write time.

### Exact value sets, with a cap

For a low-cardinality column (a status, a region, a product category) you can store the actual set of distinct values in each file. Then `status = 'FAILED'` skips any file whose set doesn't contain it, and an `IN` list checks each value. Unlike bounds, it doesn't need the column to be sorted, but it still only helps when a value is missing from many files: rare values, or data that's clustered by something correlated with it.

The cap is the whole design. Above some number of distinct values the set stops being cheap, so the writer gives up and records "too many to list". That marker has to mean **maybe**, and it has to stay maybe through every merge, until the index is rebuilt from the data. More on that below.

**When they pay:** equality and `IN` filters on columns with tens to low thousands of distinct values per file. In practice a single well-chosen value set can account for most of the skipping on a table.

### Bloom filters

For high-cardinality columns where you look up one value at a time (IDs, keys, hashes), a value set would be as big as the column. A bloom filter answers "definitely not here" or "maybe" in a fixed number of bits.

The mechanics fit in a paragraph. Allocate *m* bits. To insert a value, hash it *k* ways and set those *k* bits. To query, check the same *k* bits: if any is zero, the value was never inserted. For a target false-positive rate *p* you need about 1.44 × log₂(1/*p*) bits per distinct value, so around 9.6 bits for 1%, with *k* ≈ 7.

The useful way to reason about a bloom filter after the fact is its **fill**: the fraction of bits set. The false-positive rate is roughly fill to the power *k*. A filter that's half full with *k* = 7 answers "maybe" for an absent value about 1% of the time. A filter that's 90% full does so about half the time, and at that point it's paying its storage and a read to tell you almost nothing.

**When they pay:** point lookups and small `IN` lists on high-cardinality columns. Parquet supports them per column chunk, as split-block filters that need a few more bits for the same rate, though most writers leave them off ([bloom filters at the scan](https://sriv.github.io/notes/bloom-filters-at-the-scan/) is about that).

**When they don't:** range predicates, `LIKE '%x%'`, anything that isn't equality. And columns where every file contains most values anyway.

### Inverted indexes

For text, the question is "which rows contain this token?". An inverted index answers it with two parts.

The **term dictionary** maps each distinct token to where its postings live. A good choice for an immutable file is a finite-state transducer (FST): a minimal automaton over the sorted terms that shares both prefixes and suffixes, so a dictionary of millions of terms is often a fraction of the raw strings, and it supports prefix and range lookups for free. Lucene uses one as the index into its term dictionary, and Tantivy uses one as the dictionary itself.

The **postings** are, for each term, the set of row positions containing it. Compressed bitmaps such as Roaring are the usual format: they pick a sparse array, a dense bitmap or a run-length representation per block of 65,536 positions, and intersecting two of them for `a AND b` is fast.

Unlike the structures above, an inverted index locates rows rather than ruling out chunks. The scan still opens the file, but it only decodes the pages that hold rows the bitmap names, and only materialises those rows.

**When they pay:** token search over text, where neither bounds nor value sets can help.

**When they don't:** they're the biggest of these structures, and the most frequent terms have the biggest postings while being the least useful for skipping, since they're in every file anyway. Any real inverted index needs a size budget, and that budget raises a correctness question I come back to below.

### Sketches

Some structures don't skip anything. A HyperLogLog or theta sketch estimates how many distinct values a column has in a few kilobytes, and sketches from different files merge into a sketch of the union.

Their job is to feed the optimizer: join order, aggregation strategy and memory sizing all depend on cardinality. A sketch that's off by 2x doesn't return a wrong result. It quietly picks worse plans, which is harder to notice.

### Value-to-file maps

At the partition level you can invert the value set: for each value, a bitmap of which files in the partition contain it. One small read at planning time then narrows hundreds of files to the handful worth opening, without touching any per-file index.

This is the structure that addresses the "opened a thousand files to find three" problem directly. Its cost is that it has to be maintained as files come and go, and it needs the same cap-and-give-up rule as value sets.

## Choosing

| The predicate looks like | Data layout | Reach for |
|---|---|---|
| range on a time or sequence column | sorted or clustered | min/max bounds, which you already have |
| equality or `IN` on a low-cardinality column | rare values, or clustered | value sets, with a cap |
| equality on an ID or key | any | bloom filters per file or row group |
| token in a text column | any | inverted index or token blooms |
| "which files have value *x*?" across many files | any | value-to-file map at the partition |
| nothing, it's the optimizer asking | any | sketches |

Two questions decide most cases before any of this. Is the skipping limited by layout, so that sorting the data would make the free bounds work? And at which level is the cost: in files opened, or in rows decoded?

## Where they live: Iceberg Puffin

Parquet and Iceberg manifests already carry bounds and counts. Anything beyond that needs a home, and Iceberg's answer is **Puffin**.

A Puffin file is deliberately simple. It starts with the four magic bytes `PFA1`, then any number of **blobs** (opaque byte ranges), then a footer: the magic again, a JSON payload describing every blob, the payload's length, four bytes of flags, and the magic once more. A reader fetches the end of the file, finds the footer, and from the JSON learns each blob's type, byte range, compression codec, the columns it covers, and the snapshot it was computed for. Each blob has its own offset and length and is compressed on its own, so a reader fetches only the blobs it needs, with ranged reads.

The spec defines two blob types:

- **`apache-datasketches-theta-v1`**: a theta sketch of a column's distinct values, with the estimate also stored as a property for readers that don't want to deserialize the sketch.
- **`deletion-vector-v1`**: a serialized 64-bit Roaring bitmap of deleted row positions in one data file, with a length, magic bytes and a checksum around it, introduced with the v3 format.

Table metadata points to Puffin files through **statistics** entries, each tied to one snapshot and listing the blobs it holds. That's the important detail for anyone planning to put skipping indexes in Puffin: the spec's statistics are table-level and tied to a snapshot. Deletion vectors are the exception: each one has its own entry in a delete manifest, which names the data file it applies to and the byte range of its blob. For a custom per-file or per-partition index, the format is ready (any blob type you like, read with a ranged request) but where the files live and how a reader finds them is the engine's decision. And an index written for snapshot *n* says nothing about files added in *n*+1.

## What building them taught me

Most of what went wrong this year wasn't in the structures themselves. It was in the plumbing around them: what happens when a build is incomplete, when files are compacted, when two copies of an index disagree. Each lesson below came from a real bug or a near miss.

[Diagram: False-positive rate of a bloom filter built by OR-ing per-file blooms, each 1% full with seven hash functions. It stays near zero for small unions, reaches about 4% at 100 files, and about 70% at 300 files.]

*A union of small, healthy blooms is a large, saturated one.*

**An incomplete index is a lying index.** If the index is built while writing, and the indexer falls behind and skips even one batch, the result says "not here" about values that are there. The safe responses are to throw the index away or mark it "maybe" for the whole file. A missing index costs performance. A partial one costs correctness.

**Caps must degrade to "maybe", and stay there through merges.** When two files merge, their value sets union. If either side had given up, the merged set has given up too, even if the values that were recorded add up to only a few. The ones that weren't recorded are still in the data. Re-applying the cap on a union of two incomplete sets produces a confident, wrong answer.

**Unions of bloom filters fill up.** Two bloom filters merge with a bitwise OR, but only if they have the same size and hash functions. And the union of *N* filters is fuller than any of them: with per-file fill *f*, the union's fill is 1 − (1 − *f*)^*N*. If every per-file filter is sized for the partition (so they can be OR-ed) and so is 1% full, with *k* = 7, a union of 100 files is about 63% full and gives a false positive about 4% of the time. A union of 300 is 95% full and gives a false positive 70% of the time. A partition-level bloom built as an OR of per-file blooms has to be sized for the partition, not the file, or it should be checked for fill before anyone trusts it. I now write a fill check next to every bloom: above a threshold, don't emit it, and on the read side, don't trust it.

**Compaction is where indexes go to die.** When small files merge into big ones, each index has three options: carry it forward (rebase row positions, union the sets), rebuild it from the merged rows, or drop it. Dropping is safe but silent: queries just get slower and nobody knows why. Carrying forward is cheap but has to respect every rule above. Rebuilding is the most expensive and the most correct. The bug I least want to repeat was a merge that kept the **wrong copy** of an index when two generations existed for the same file, and the reader then skipped files that matched. A stale index is worse than none.

**A budget needs a record of what it dropped.** An inverted index with a size budget will drop terms, usually the frequent ones. If the reader can't tell "this term never appeared" from "this term was dropped", the budget has turned into false negatives. Whatever drops entries has to leave enough behind for the reader to know to fall back to a scan.

**Hashes must be stable across builds.** Sketches and blooms built by one build of the writer get merged with ones built by the next. If the hash function isn't specified (a language's default hasher, for example, which may change between compiler versions), merged structures silently stop agreeing. Pick a hash with a written specification and pin it.

**Count requests, not just bytes.** A reader that fetches one small index file per data file can spend more time on index requests than the index saves. This is why the partition-level structures exist, and why a single read of a small file beats several ranged reads of it.

**Test the property, not the example.** Example-based tests of these structures pass easily, because examples are small and friendly. What found real bugs for me was randomized property testing with replayable seeds: for any random set of values, nothing inserted is ever reported absent; a union reports every member of every input; the parser never crashes on arbitrary bytes. That suite found a crash in a footer parser on malformed input, and a sketch that roughly doubled its estimates above a certain cardinality, hidden below it by the small-range correction every test happened to exercise.

## The short version

Indexes in an analytical engine are mostly a hierarchy of cheap questions, each one asked so that a more expensive question never has to be. Pick the granularity where the cost is, pick the structure the predicate needs, store it where the reader can fetch it in one request, and treat every way it can go stale or incomplete as a correctness bug, because that's what it is.

---

# Simulating the commit path: deterministic tests for streaming writes to Iceberg

By Srikanth Venugopalan, 13 August 2026. Topics: testing, iceberg, distributed.
Canonical: https://sriv.github.io/notes/simulating-the-commit-path/

> A streaming writer commits to an Iceberg table every few seconds, retries on conflict, and shares the table with compaction and garbage collection. I borrowed SlateDB's approach to deterministic simulation to test it. It caught less than I hoped, and taught me more.

A streaming writer is a very persistent client of a table format. It lands a few files, commits, and does it again a few seconds later, forever. Around it, other processes rewrite the same table: compaction merges small files, garbage collection deletes files nothing points to, snapshot expiry trims history. Every one of them commits through the same optimistic protocol: read the current metadata, write new metadata, swap a pointer, and retry from the top if someone else got there first.

Each of those steps is simple. The bugs live in the interleavings: a retry that rebuilds its change from stale state, a garbage collector that sees a file a moment before the commit that references it lands, a clock that disagrees with another clock. They show up in production as a handful of rows read twice, or a file deleted that a snapshot still needs. They almost never show up in a unit test, because a unit test runs one interleaving, the friendly one.

This summer I built a deterministic simulation harness for that commit path. This note is about how it works, what it found, and, more usefully, what it didn't.

## The idea, borrowed

The approach isn't mine. FoundationDB made deterministic simulation famous, TigerBeetle and others built on it, and tools like [madsim](https://github.com/madsim-rs/madsim) and [Antithesis](https://antithesis.com/docs/resources/deterministic_simulation_testing/) generalised it. The version I learnt the most from was [SlateDB's `slatedb-dst`](https://github.com/slatedb/slatedb/tree/main/slatedb-dst), because it solves almost the same problem: a storage engine whose only durable state lives in object storage.

Its shape is worth copying:

- **One seed decides everything.** A root random generator derives the seeds for the runtime, the clock and every actor, so a failing run can be replayed exactly from one number.
- **The world is simulated.** A mock clock instead of the system clock, a deterministic filesystem standing in for object storage, and a single-threaded runtime so scheduling is reproducible.
- **Faults are part of the world.** An object store wrapper injects latency, dropped connections and errors with seeded probabilities.
- **Invariants, not examples.** The flagship test is a bank: actors transfer money between accounts while an auditor checks that the total never changes, through every kind of reader.
- **Determinism is itself tested.** The same seed is run twice and the runs must agree. Otherwise the harness is quietly testing something else.
- **It runs all the time.** SlateDB runs its simulations in CI every hour.

[Diagram: Deterministic simulation: one seed drives a simulated clock, an object store with seeded faults, and actors such as writers, garbage collection and snapshot expiry. They exercise the real commit path, and an oracle checks invariants after every step. A failing run prints its seed, so it can be replayed exactly.]

*Everything that can vary comes from the seed, so every failure can be replayed.*

## Two tiers

I ended up with two kinds of simulation, and the distinction turned out to matter more than anything else.

### Models of the protocol

The first tier doesn't run the real code at all. It's a few hundred lines of plain Rust that model one piece of the commit protocol: a table as a set of files, a catalog as a pointer, writers and collectors as actors taking seeded steps. No dependencies, a tiny seeded generator, and a function that runs a schedule and returns the first invariant it breaks.

Each model comes as a pair:

- a **naive** version of the algorithm, which the harness must catch breaking the invariant on many seeds, and
- a **safe** version, which must hold the invariant on every seed.

The pairing keeps the harness honest. If the naive version stops failing, the simulation has lost its teeth, not found a fix.

The models covered the commit races I cared about:

- **Commit against garbage collection.** Invariant: every file reachable from the table exists in storage. The naive collector deletes anything currently unreachable, which includes files written by a commit that hasn't landed yet. The safe one waits out a grace period.
- **Optimistic retry of a rewrite.** Invariant: the table's content never changes across a rewrite, and the files stay a partition of it, with no row in two files. The naive retry reuses the list of files it decided to remove before the conflict.
- **At-least-once delivery.** A consumer that deduplicates by message id turns at-least-once into exactly-once. One that doesn't, doesn't.
- **Clock skew.** A grace period measured in wall-clock time is defeated by a collector whose clock runs ahead. A guard based on the catalog's own sequence numbers isn't, because it never asks anyone what time it is.

That last one is my favourite result of the whole exercise. It turned a vague worry ("what if clocks drift?") into a precise rule: never let a correctness decision depend on two machines agreeing about time.

I want to be honest about what this tier is, though. Every one of those models reproduces a bug we'd already had or already feared. They're **executable specifications of known failures**. That's valuable: the rule is now written down in a form that fails loudly, and the next person to touch the protocol inherits it. But it isn't discovery.

### The real code, under faults

The second tier runs the real table library: the real transaction and its retry loop, the real manifest writer, the real scan planner, in-process against an in-memory catalog and file system. Seeded schedules mix appends, rewrites and expiries, and after every commit the test checks the table against an **oracle**, a plain set of the files that should be live:

- nothing lost and nothing duplicated: the scan returns exactly the oracle's files,
- a failed commit leaves the table unchanged,
- the reachable set is exactly the set of successful commits, with no phantoms,
- after expiring every older snapshot, the current one is still fully readable.

Faults come from two wrappers. One fails the catalog's register step, which models a crash after the files are written but before the commit is recorded. The other sits under the file system and fails reads, writes and deletes, adds latency, or partitions the network until healed.

My favourite invariant in this tier is a small one: **a read fault must surface as an error, never as fewer rows.** A scan that swallows a failed read and returns a short result is the worst kind of bug in an analytical engine, because nothing about the answer looks wrong.

## What it caught

Less than I'd hoped. And the best catch was one I ignored.

**The signal I misread.** One of the first real-code tests appended three files in one commit, replaced two of them with a merged file, and expected the merged file plus the untouched one. On one format version it failed: the replaced files stayed live. I'd only just built the harness, the failure involved a code path I was less sure the test set up correctly, and I concluded the harness was wrong. I marked the test ignored and moved on.

Two months later the same bug turned up the expensive way. When a rewrite touched a manifest that mixed files being replaced with files being kept, it wrote every entry back as newly *added*, including the ones that should have been marked *deleted*. The replaced files stayed live next to their replacement, so every merged row was read twice. The snapshot summary still reported the deletes, which made it look fine to anything that only read the summary. Looking back, the regression test written for the fix has almost exactly the shape of the test I'd ignored in August. To be sure, I ran the August test, unchanged, against the code from just before the fix. It fails exactly as it did then, with the two replaced files still live next to their replacement. On the fixed code, it passes.

The harness did its job. I didn't do mine. The lesson I took is now a rule: **a red simulation test is a bug until proven otherwise**, and "the harness is probably wrong" needs the same evidence as "the code is wrong".

**A safety switch wired to nothing.** Writing a test for conflicting rewrites, I found a flag meant to disable retries for exactly that case. The retry logic read it. Nothing ever set it. It had been wired up after an earlier incident, then unwired when a better fix made retries safe, and the flag was left behind looking like protection. It wasn't a live bug, but it's the kind of thing only a test that tries to use the switch will find.

**The harness that tested nothing.** After a dependency upgrade, the in-memory file system stopped going through the I/O layer the fault injector was attached to. Every fault test kept passing, because no fault ever reached the code under test. The fix was to wrap the storage at the level the commit and scan paths actually call, and to make sure the wrapper hands back wrapped readers and writers rather than the inner ones. That's the reason for SlateDB's determinism test, and I'd now add a cousin to every harness: **a test that proves the faults are landing**, by checking that the naive version still fails.

## What it doesn't do

This is the part I'd want to read if someone else had written this note.

- **It's barely concurrent.** The real-code tier has no simulated scheduler. Races are staged by hand: two transactions from the same starting point. The interleavings it explores are the ones I thought of.
- **Time isn't simulated in the real code.** The library still asks the system clock. Clock skew is tested with synthetic timestamps, which is weaker than owning the clock.
- **Too few seeds, too rarely.** A dozen seeds per test, run with the normal test suite. No soak runs, no hourly job, no way to throw a million seeds at it overnight. SlateDB does all three.
- **The oracle is too coarse.** It tracks which files should be live, not what rows they hold, and the schedules for one format version never included rewrites at all. That gap is exactly where the missed bug lived.
- **No real catalog, no real crash.** The catalog is in memory, so there's no network between the writer and its commit. And the streaming writer itself never crashes and restarts inside the simulation, which is where exactly-once really gets tested.

Most of that list is one piece of work: threading a clock and a storage interface through the writer and the catalog client, so the simulation can own both. That's the line between "tests with seeds" and a simulation, and SlateDB is on the right side of it.

## What I'd do again

- **Pair every model with a naive version that must fail.** It's the cheapest way to know the harness can still see.
- **Make "never fewer rows" an invariant.** Silent short reads are the bug analytical systems can't afford.
- **Prefer logical clocks for correctness.** Anything that compares wall-clock times across machines will eventually be wrong.
- **Treat red as real.** The most valuable output of a simulation is a failure you don't yet understand. It deserves more time, not less.
- **Run it constantly.** A simulation that runs a dozen seeds once per pull request is a unit test with extra steps. The value is in the volume.

---

# An Iceberg catalog with no database: Lakekeeper on SlateDB

By Srikanth Venugopalan, 17 June 2026. Topics: iceberg, lakehouse, storage.
Canonical: https://sriv.github.io/notes/a-catalog-on-object-storage/

> I wrote a backend that keeps an Iceberg REST catalog's state in SlateDB, a key-value store that lives entirely in object storage. It worked, and it kept the catalog's state out of a database. This note is mostly about what it cost: the guarantees I rebuilt, the ones I didn't, and what I'd do differently.

An Iceberg table is files in object storage plus one pointer: the location of the current metadata file. Everything else in a lakehouse can be scaled, cached or thrown away and rebuilt. That pointer can't. Every writer swaps it with a compare-and-swap, and the catalog is the thing that owns the swap.

[Lakekeeper](https://github.com/lakekeeper/lakekeeper) is an open-source Iceberg REST catalog written in Rust. The server is stateless and keeps its state in Postgres. That's a sensible default, and for most people the right one. But it does mean that a system whose data lives entirely in object storage still needs a database next to it, with its own backups, upgrades, failover and on-call.

[SlateDB](https://slatedb.io) is an embedded key-value store that writes everything, its write-ahead log included, to object storage. No disks to manage, no replicas to run. So the obvious question: can the catalog live in the same bucket as the tables it describes?

I built a SlateDB backend for Lakekeeper to find out. It runs, it passes about 170 tests, and I learnt more from its limitations than from the parts that worked.

## Why bother

The motivation wasn't performance. Postgres is faster at almost everything a catalog does. It was operational:

- **One durable system, not two.** If the tables and the catalog live in the same object store, durability, replication and backup are one problem, solved by the cloud provider.
- **Nothing stateful to run.** The catalog becomes a process that can be killed and restarted anywhere, as long as only one copy writes at a time.
- **Cost proportional to use.** A catalog that serves a few commits a minute doesn't need a database instance sized for peak.

## What a backend has to implement

Lakekeeper's backend is chosen at compile time: you hand a storage type to the server. The contract is a set of Rust traits, and it's much bigger than "store table metadata":

- a **transaction** trait: begin a read or write transaction, commit, roll back;
- a **catalog store** trait with close to a hundred async methods: projects, warehouses, namespaces, tables, views, generic tables, roles, users, role memberships (transitive, paginated), endpoint statistics, a **task queue**, and idempotency keys;
- a **secret store** for storage credentials.

The Postgres backend leans on SQL for almost all of it, and each of those SQL features became something I had to rebuild by hand.

| Postgres gives you | On a key-value store, I had to build |
|---|---|
| A table commit as one `UPDATE … WHERE metadata_location = old` | A read, a compare, and a write |
| `UNIQUE` constraints, case-insensitive | Name-index keys, checked before insert |
| Secondary indexes | About twenty hand-maintained index key families |
| `ORDER BY … LIMIT` with a cursor | Prefix scans plus pagination tokens |
| Recursive queries over role membership | Graph walks in memory |
| `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` for the task queue | A scan for the first scheduled task |
| Trigram search | Substring match over a scan |
| `ALTER TABLE` and migrations | Versioned rewrite functions run at startup |

## How it's built

**Keys are paths.** Every record has a primary key (`table/{id}`, `ns/{id}`, `warehouse/{id}`) and one or more index keys that point at it (`table_by_name/{warehouse}/{namespace}/{name}`, `table_by_metadata_loc/{location}`, and so on). Names come from users, so every user-supplied segment is percent-encoded before it goes into a key. My first encoding replaced a few characters and could make two different names collide. Fixing that needed a migration that rebuilt every index. In a key-value store, the key encoding is the schema, and I learnt that the expensive way.

**Records are JSON.** Postgres splits Iceberg table metadata across about fifteen normalised tables. I stored the whole metadata document in the table's record. Simpler, and fine for a catalog that mostly reads and replaces the whole thing.

**A transaction is a buffer.** Each request collects its puts and deletes and writes them at commit as one atomic batch. That's what keeps a record and its indexes from ever being half-written. Reads inside the transaction merge the pending buffer over the database, so a request sees its own writes. The first version didn't, and a request that created something and then looked it up couldn't find it. Tests caught that in the first week.

**Migrations are code.** A schema version key, and an ordered list of functions that rewrite keys and values from one version to the next, run by the writer at startup. There's no `ALTER TABLE` in a key-value store.

## The limitations

This is the part that matters, and the reason I'd tell anyone to think hard before doing the same.

**One writer, so no high availability.** SlateDB is [designed for a single writer](https://slatedb.io/docs/get-started/introduction/) and fences out old ones with an epoch in its manifest. That's a good design, and it's what keeps two writers from corrupting each other. But it means the catalog has exactly one process that can commit. Restart it and every table in the lakehouse is read-only until it's back. Start a second copy and it fences the first instead of sharing the load. Lakekeeper on Postgres is stateless and scales horizontally. On SlateDB, it isn't and doesn't. SlateDB supports readers on other nodes, and serving catalog reads from them is the obvious next step. I didn't build it.

**Every commit waits for object storage.** A commit is only durable once the write-ahead log has reached object storage. That's a flush interval plus a PUT, so tens to hundreds of milliseconds, where Postgres takes a few. SlateDB is upfront about this: it's [meant for workloads that tolerate 50 to 100 ms writes](https://slatedb.io/docs/get-started/introduction/). For a catalog that's acceptable. For a catalog under a streaming writer committing to hundreds of tables, it's the number to watch.

**My compare-and-swap isn't atomic.** This is the honest one. Postgres does the commit in one statement: update the pointer only if it still points where the client thinks. My backend reads the record, compares, then writes. The server is the only writer, so a lock around that path would have been enough. I didn't add one, and with many concurrent requests in one process, nothing stops two of them passing the check before either writes. The same window exists for name uniqueness and for claiming a task from the queue. And when my backend did detect a conflict, it reported a server error rather than Iceberg's 409 conflict, which a client reads as "I don't know if my commit happened" rather than "retry".

What makes this worse is that it was avoidable. SlateDB has had [transactions with snapshot and serializable-snapshot isolation](https://slatedb.io/rfcs/0011-transaction/) since late 2025, with write-write conflict detection. I built on plain write batches instead, because they were simpler and I was copying the shape of the Postgres backend. A real compare-and-swap, real uniqueness and safe task claiming are all one transaction away. If I started again, that's the first thing I'd change.

**The task queue was the sharpest edge.** Lakekeeper schedules background work, like cleaning up dropped tables, through its task queue, and some of those tasks reschedule themselves. My first port dropped the "not before this time" condition when picking tasks. Self-rescheduling tasks ran as fast as the loop could pick them, every write went to the log, the log grew, and replaying it on restart got slow enough that the process failed its health checks. A one-line filter in SQL became an outage-shaped bug in a key-value port. The queue also ignores heartbeat timeouts, so a task held by a crashed worker is never picked up again.

**Lists and searches don't scale.** Pagination scans the whole prefix and skips to the cursor, so every page costs as much as the whole list. Search is substring matching over a scan. Role inheritance is walked in memory. All of it is fine for hundreds of tables. None of it is fine for millions.

**Some things are missing.** Endpoint and warehouse statistics return nothing. Secrets are stored without encryption, which rules it out for anyone who keeps real credentials in the catalog. Authorisation through OpenFGA still needs its own database, so "no database" only holds if you don't use it.

**Operations get harder.** There's no SQL console. Debugging means reading keys by hand. Backing up by copying the prefix isn't safe while compaction is rewriting files underneath it. SlateDB has checkpoints for exactly this, but I never wired them into a backup. When something goes wrong, the answer is often "look at the log files in the bucket", which is a sentence nobody wants in a runbook.

**The interface moves.** Lakekeeper changed the backend traits a week after I finished, and the backend didn't compile until I caught up. Every upstream release is a small porting job, which is the strongest argument against keeping a backend like this outside the project.[^issue]

## What about FoundationDB?

The other backend people reach for in this conversation is [FoundationDB](https://apple.github.io/foundationdb/), and it's worth being precise about the difference, because it's the whole design space in one line. FoundationDB is a distributed key-value store with strictly serializable transactions across many writers. Putting a catalog on it gives you everything Postgres gives you except SQL: real compare-and-swap, real uniqueness, many active catalog servers, no single writer to restart. What it doesn't give you is "no stateful system to run". FoundationDB is a cluster with its own disks, coordinators and operational folklore. It's arguably harder to run than Postgres.

So the three options sit on one axis:

- **Postgres:** transactions and SQL, a database to operate.
- **FoundationDB:** transactions across many writers, a harder cluster to operate.
- **SlateDB:** nothing to operate but a bucket, at the price of a single writer and object-storage latency.

None of them is wrong. They trade operational weight for concurrency, and the right one depends on how many writers you have and how much infrastructure you're willing to own.

## What I'd tell someone starting

- **Count the contract first.** "Store the catalog in a key-value store" sounds like a table and an index. It's a hundred methods, a task queue, authorisation data and secrets.
- **Use the store's transactions.** Every hand-rolled check-then-write in this backend is a race that SlateDB's transactions would have closed.
- **Map conflicts to conflicts.** A 409 makes a client retry. Anything else makes it wonder whether its data is there.
- **Port the `WHERE` clauses, not just the tables.** The worst bug here was a time condition that didn't make the trip from SQL.
- **Decide about availability up front.** A single writer is a feature for correctness and a bug for uptime. Know which one your users will notice.

[^issue]: Months after I built this, someone proposed the same idea upstream in [lakekeeper#2079](https://github.com/lakekeeper/lakekeeper/issues/2079) (October 2026), building on SlateDB's transactions, which is the approach I'd take now. The maintainers replied that they don't have the capacity to support another backend upstream, because maintaining one is a lot of continuous effort. Having done it, I agree.

---

# A metadata tree that grows with the change

By Srikanth Venugopalan, 5 June 2026. Topics: iceberg.
Canonical: https://sriv.github.io/notes/a-metadata-tree-that-grows-with-the-change/

> The draft Iceberg v4 spec replaces the manifest list with a root manifest. It sounds like a file rename. It changes what a small commit costs.

[Manifests are data too](https://sriv.github.io/notes/manifests-are-data-too/) was about manifests becoming Parquet files. This one is about the bigger structural change in the draft version 4 of the Iceberg spec, the **adaptive metadata tree**. It's an explainer of the public spec plus what I learned implementing it. I'll only describe what's in the spec and upstream proposals, not anything specific to how we use it.

## How an Iceberg commit works today

An Iceberg table is a tree of files. At the top is a table metadata file. It points to the current snapshot, and the snapshot points to a **manifest list**. The manifest list points to **manifests**, and each manifest lists data files along with their partition values and column statistics.

A commit writes new files bottom-up and then atomically swaps the table's pointer from the old metadata file to the new one. If someone else committed first, you rebase and try again. That's the optimistic concurrency model, and it's the reason Iceberg works on plain object storage without table locks: the only coordination is one atomic swap in the catalog.

Now look at what a small append writes in versions 1 to 3:

1. the new data file,
2. a new manifest listing it (this is what a fast append does),
3. a **new manifest list** containing an entry for *every* manifest in the snapshot,
4. a new table metadata file.

Step 3 is the problem. The manifest list is rewritten on every commit, and its size grows with the number of manifests in the table, not with the size of the change. A writer that frequently appends small batches keeps adding manifests, so each commit rewrites a slightly bigger list than the last. Eventually the manifests have to be merged, either inline during some commits, which makes those commits bigger, or by a background rewrite, which is another writer competing for the same commit pointer.

The cost of a commit ends up tracking the size of the table's metadata rather than the size of the change. For tables that are mostly read and occasionally written that's fine. For tables that take a steady stream of small appends it becomes the bottleneck.

## The root manifest

Version 4 removes the manifest list. Each snapshot points to a single **root manifest**, which is itself a manifest, and it can hold three kinds of entries:

- data files, directly,
- **leaf manifests**, which hold data files,
- older v1–v3 manifests, so existing tables can be upgraded without rewriting history.

Root and leaf manifests written in v4 are Parquet files, not Avro, which was the subject of the previous post.

[Diagram: In Iceberg v1 to v3, table metadata points to a manifest list that is rewritten on every commit and has one entry per manifest, so a small append writes a new manifest and a growing list. In v4, table metadata points to a Parquet root manifest that holds leaf manifests and can hold data files directly; small appends go straight into the root, and a deletion bitmap on the root's entry marks files in a leaf as removed without rewriting the leaf.]

*The manifest list grows with the table. The root manifest grows with the change, as long as someone keeps it small.*

The important part is the first kind of entry. A small append no longer needs its own manifest *and* a rewritten list. Its data files can go straight into the root. The commit writes the data file, one new root manifest, and the table metadata. Later, when the root has accumulated enough loose files, a writer can move them down into a leaf manifest, and the root goes back to holding a short list of pointers.

That's what "adaptive" means here. The tree is shallow where things change often and deeper where they don't. The spec defines the structure. It deliberately doesn't say when to push files down, how big a root should get, or how leaves should be grouped. Those are implementation choices, and they're where most of the engineering is.

## Removing an entry without rewriting a leaf

The second piece is about deletes and compaction. In v1–v3, if compaction replaces ten small files with one big one, every manifest that listed those ten files has to be rewritten without them.

Version 4 adds **manifest deletion vectors**. The root manifest's entry for a leaf can carry a bitmap of positions in that leaf that are no longer live. Removing a file from a leaf means setting bits on the root entry, while the leaf itself stays untouched. The bitmaps use [Mumbling](https://iceberg.apache.org/mumbling-spec/), a compact bitmap encoding the Iceberg project specifies for this, and the root entry records which snapshot last changed them.

The same idea shows up one level down. A data file's own deletion vector, the bitmap of deleted rows inside it, now lives in the same manifest entry as the data file. For files written under v4, readers no longer have to plan in two phases, finding data files first and then doing a second lookup to match delete files to them. The deletes sit in the same entry as the file they apply to, so planning reads one thing instead of joining two.

## Smaller changes that matter to implementers

A few other v4 rules changed how I wrote code more than I expected:

- **Strictly increasing snapshot timestamps.** On a v4 table, a snapshot's timestamp must be strictly greater than its parent's on the same branch. Two fast writers on machines with slightly different clocks can break that, so the commit path has to compare against the parent and bump the timestamp past it when the local clock hasn't moved far enough, rather than trusting the machine's time.
- **Relative paths.** Metadata can store file locations relative to the table location, which makes copying or moving a table much less painful.
- **No new equality deletes.** Writers can't produce new equality delete files in v4. Existing ones stay readable.
- **Sequence numbers are still inherited.** As in v2 and v3, files added to a new leaf manifest are written without a sequence number, and readers fill it in from the root manifest's entry for that leaf. That's what lets a writer write a leaf manifest once and reuse it across commit retries. Only the root has to be rewritten when the commit is retried.

## What I learned implementing it

**The spec gives you the shape, not the policy.** Every interesting decision is about *when*: when to push loose files into leaves, when a leaf is too big, when to fold manifest deletion vectors back into a rewritten leaf. Get the policy wrong and you can rebuild the very problem v4 set out to fix, a root that grows with the table.

**The retry path is the real commit path.** Under optimistic concurrency, retries aren't a corner case. With several writers they're routine. Most of the bugs I found weren't in the happy path. They were in what a retry reuses, what it recomputes, and what it must validate again against the new base snapshot.

**Write down the invariants and test them on purpose.** The spec says each file must appear in at most one live entry across the snapshot, and it explicitly doesn't require writers to check that at commit time. That's a reasonable spec decision, and it means the checking is on you. Randomized sequences of appends, compactions and retries, checked against a written-down list of invariants, are the cheapest way I know to find the bugs that hide in retries.

---

# Manifests are data too

By Srikanth Venugopalan, 13 May 2026. Topics: iceberg.
Canonical: https://sriv.github.io/notes/manifests-are-data-too/

> Iceberg's manifests have always been row-oriented Avro. The draft version 4 spec makes them Parquet. Everything I'd learned about not reading data turned out to apply to metadata as well.

This year I moved down a layer. After two years inside query engines, deciding what not to read, I started working on the table format underneath them: [Apache Iceberg](https://iceberg.apache.org/), and specifically the metadata changes going into version 4 of its spec.

The first piece I implemented was the smallest-sounding one: writing **manifests** as Parquet instead of Avro. At the time it was a proposal under discussion upstream. It has since been merged into the v4 draft of the spec, which hasn't been formally adopted yet. This post is about why such a dull-sounding change matters, and why it helped commits as well as queries.

## What a manifest is, and who reads it

An Iceberg manifest is a list of files. Each entry describes one data file: its path, partition values, row count, and statistics for its columns (lower and upper bounds, null counts and so on).

Two kinds of readers open manifests:

- **Query planning** reads them to decide which data files a query needs, using the partition values and column bounds. This is the pruning ladder from [the cheapest row is the one you never read](https://sriv.github.io/notes/the-cheapest-row-is-the-one-you-never-read/), one level up.
- **Commits** read them too, which is easy to forget. A compaction has to confirm the files it's replacing are still in the table. A retried commit has to look at what changed underneath it. A delete or overwrite needs the record counts of the files it removes, for the snapshot summary.

In versions 1 to 3, a manifest is an Avro file, which stores data row by row. To get any field of an entry, you still have to read through the whole entry, because there's no way to jump straight to one field.

## Where Avro hurts

The column statistics are where it shows. In v1–v3 each entry stores them as maps from column ID to a value: one map for lower bounds, one for upper bounds, more for null counts, value counts and sizes. The bounds are stored as bytes, which the reader then has to decode according to each column's type.

Picture a wide table with a few hundred columns and a query that filters on one of them. Every manifest entry carries bound maps for every column that has metrics enabled, which by default is the first hundred, and planning decodes all of it to find the one pair of bounds it needs. Most of the bytes read during planning belong to columns the query never mentions.

It's the same problem as reading rows you don't need, just in metadata instead of data. And the fix is the same one.

## Parquet manifests

In v4, manifests are Parquet files. The statistics change shape too. Instead of maps of bytes, each table column gets its own typed struct inside a `content_stats` field. A column's bounds are stored as that column's real type, so an `int` column has `int` bounds.

Each stats struct gets a fixed block of 200 field IDs, starting at `10_000 + 200 × field-id`. That leaves room for every metric a column can have, including nested ones like geospatial bounds. A reader that wants the bounds for column 2 knows exactly which Parquet columns hold them, without looking at anything else.

[Diagram: An Avro manifest stores each file entry as a row, with column statistics in maps over every column, so finding one column's bounds decodes every entry in full. A Parquet manifest stores each field as a column, so a filter on c2 reads only the path column and c2's typed statistics. Commits benefit too, since they read narrow slices such as paths, statuses and counts.]

*Same manifest, two layouts. Planning and commits both want a few columns of it, not all of it.*

That buys three things:

- **Projection.** Planning reads only the stats columns for the columns in the filter, plus the path. The rest of the manifest stays on disk.
- **No per-type byte parsing.** Bounds come out as typed values, already in the right representation.
- **Pruning inside metadata.** A Parquet manifest has its own row-group statistics. A large manifest whose entries are clustered, for example by partition, can skip whole chunks of them before decoding, using the same min/max machinery we use on data.

## Why commits got cheaper

The query-side win is the obvious one. The commit-side win surprised me more.

Most of what a commit reads from existing manifests is narrow. Validating a compaction mostly needs paths and statuses. Rebasing a retry needs to know which entries changed. Updating the summary needs the record counts of removed files. With Avro, each of those still decoded whole entries, statistics maps included. With Parquet, each reads the one or two columns it needs.

Writing got better too. Manifest columns are very repetitive (long, similar file paths, the same partition values, similar row counts), and columnar encoding and compression handle that far better than compressing blocks of whole rows, which is what Avro does. Smaller manifests are cheaper to write, upload and read back on the next commit.

A commit is a chain of small reads and writes against object storage, and every one of them sits inside the window where another writer can beat you to it. Making each step touch fewer bytes makes the window shorter, and a shorter window means fewer retries.

## What it costs

Parquet isn't free, and it's worth being honest about where it loses:

- **Tiny files pay a fixed tax.** A Parquet file has a footer, a schema and per-column overhead. A manifest with three entries can come out bigger in Parquet than in Avro.
- **The schema depends on the table.** Because `content_stats` has one struct per table column, the manifest schema is built from the table schema. Schema evolution has to be handled carefully, which is why the spec says stats are resolved by ID and names are informational only.
- **Readers have to change.** Every engine that reads manifests needs a Parquet path. While the proposal was still being discussed, I kept the new format behind a switch, so tables could be moved over deliberately rather than all at once.

## What I'd tell someone implementing it

- **Treat metadata as data.** Everything you know about columnar layout, projection and pruning applies. It's easy to forget, because metadata files feel small, until a table has millions of them.
- **Look at the commit path, not just planning.** The reads a commit does are narrow and frequent, and they're exactly the kind columnar formats are good at.
- **Round-trip every type.** Bounds for floats (where `NaN` can never be a bound and is counted separately, and `-0.0` must sort before `+0.0` even though they compare equal), decimals, timestamps and strings all have edge cases. A test that writes and reads back every type is cheap, and it's worth writing before anything else.
- **Build ahead of a spec behind a switch.** Implementing a proposal early teaches you a lot, but the format will change before it's final, and you don't want existing tables quietly committed to your first guess.

---

# Porting an idea, not the code

By Srikanth Venugopalan, 18 December 2025. Topics: rust, datafusion, indexes.
Canonical: https://sriv.github.io/notes/porting-an-idea-not-the-code/

> Bringing dynamic indexes from a Java engine to one built on Rust and DataFusion. What carried over was a handful of rules. Almost none of the code did.

By the end of 2025 the team was building a native executor in Rust on top of [Apache DataFusion](https://datafusion.apache.org/). I'd spent a good part of the previous year on dynamic indexes in our Java engine ([the post on lazily built indexes](https://sriv.github.io/notes/let-the-queries-build-the-index/)), so in December I took on bringing them across.

I expected a translation job and got something closer to a redesign. Writing an idea a second time, in a different engine, shows you which parts of it were the idea and which parts were just how the first engine happened to be built.

## What carried over

Here's what survived the trip unchanged. None of it is code:

- **An index answers "maybe" or "no", and a wrong "no" is the only real bug.** Missing entries, failed builds and anything unexpected all mean "maybe".
- **Build lazily, from data the query was reading anyway.** No background jobs, no separate build step.
- **Key everything by file and row group.** Files in a table format don't change once written, so an entry for a given file stays true.
- **An index built from a partial view of the data must never be kept.** This was the rule that mattered most in Rust, for reasons below.

Everything else was rewritten from scratch, and it should have been. The Java implementation was shaped around the Java engine's scan operator, its threading and its caches. Translating it line by line would have brought all of that along into an engine that works differently.

## Use the host's extension points

DataFusion is built to be extended, and the most useful decision in the port was to lean on that instead of fighting it.

DataFusion already knows how to prune Parquet row groups. Given a query's filter, it builds a **pruning predicate**, then asks a statistics provider for each row group's min, max, null and row counts, and whether it could contain a given set of values and works out which row groups can't possibly match. The provider is an interface. DataFusion ships one that reads the Parquet footer, but nothing stops you from supplying your own.

So the dynamic index became exactly that: a statistics provider backed by our index store. Our code answers "what's the min and max of this column in row group 3 of this file?", "could it contain 42?", or "I don't know", and DataFusion's existing logic does the rest: `AND`, `OR`, `IN`, ranges and the common forms of negation, and anything it can't rewrite becomes "maybe". In the Java engine I'd written and tested that predicate logic myself. Here I got it for free, along with everyone else's bug fixes.

The other half was the scan itself. Rather than fork DataFusion's Parquet source, I wrapped it: our source holds the stock one and passes every call through, except opening a file, where it narrows the list of row groups to read before handing over. My first cut copied more of the stock source than it needed to. The rewrite later that day was mostly deleting those copies and passing calls through.

[Diagram: Row groups in a Parquet file pass through three checks in order: our in-memory dynamic index, the footer min/max statistics, then Parquet bloom filters. Each check removes some row groups. The rest are decoded with filters pushed down, so the output is not the whole row group, and a partial view must never become an index.]

*Cheapest check first. DataFusion does the predicate logic; the dynamic index only has to answer questions about row groups.*

The order of the checks matters. Our index lives in memory, so it goes first. The footer statistics come next, since the footer has already been read. Parquet's own bloom filters come after that, because checking them means fetching more bytes, and page-index pruning after them. Each check only sees the row groups the cheaper ones before it let through.

## The filter that moved

This is where the port taught me something about the original.

In the Java engine, the scan decoded a row group into batches and a separate filter operator dropped rows afterwards. Whatever the scan produced was the whole row group. Building an index from it was safe almost by accident, because nothing upstream had thrown rows away.

DataFusion can drop rows inside the Parquet reader itself: filter pushdown evaluates predicates while decoding, and page-index pruning skips whole pages before decoding starts. That's a real performance win, and you want it on. It also means the batches that come out of the scan are no longer the row group. They're the part of the row group the current query cared about. Build a min/max or a bloom filter from that, and you've built an index that will confidently say "no" to values that are sitting right there in the file.

In Java this rule had been met by the shape of the engine. In Rust it had to be enforced deliberately: an index is only kept when we know it was built from the whole row group, and anything less is discarded. I won't go into the mechanism here. The important part is being able to name the rule. Once you can say "never keep an index built from a partial view", a whole class of bugs becomes something you check for rather than something you stumble into.

## A simpler bloom filter

The first Rust version fed values into a bloom filter with a separate branch for each column type, and only covered a handful of types. In January I replaced it with a simpler design: hash every value to a 64-bit number first, whatever its type, and keep a bloom filter of those hashes.

That one change removed a surprising amount of code:

- **No type-specific logic.** Integers, strings, dates and decimals all go through the same filter once they're hashed.
- **Uniform size.** Every filter for a given expected row count and false-positive rate is the same size, which makes memory accounting predictable.
- **Mergeable.** Two filters of the same size and hash scheme combine with a bitwise OR, so filters built in pieces can be joined without going back to the data.

The one thing to be careful of is that the hash has to be stable and has to agree between the side that builds the filter and the side that probes it. Hash `5` as an `INT` when you build the filter, probe it with the `BIGINT` literal the query planner produced, and you get a wrong "no". It's the same bug from [the bloom filter post](https://sriv.github.io/notes/bloom-filters-at-the-scan/) in different clothes.

## What I'd tell someone porting a subsystem

- **Write down the rules before you write any code.** The list above came from asking "what would make this wrong?", not from reading the old code.
- **Look for the rules the old system enforced by accident.** They're the ones a new engine breaks quietly.
- **Prefer the host's extension points to a fork.** You inherit its correctness and its future fixes, and your own code gets smaller.
- **Expect the second version to be simpler.** If it isn't, you may be porting the first engine's shape rather than the idea.

---

# Random order is only useful if you can replay it

By Srikanth Venugopalan, 6 November 2025. Topics: gauge, testing, cli design.
Canonical: https://sriv.github.io/notes/gauge-reproducible-randomness/

> In 2017 I removed a flag that ran Gauge specs in random order. In 2025 I added it back. The difference was a seed, and a place to keep it.

On 6 November 2025 I merged a [change to Gauge](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/pull/2794) that lets you run specs and scenarios in random order:

```
gauge run --sort=random specs/
Randomizing execution with seed: 1761802692487777000
```

Eight years earlier I had [removed a flag that did much the same thing](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/pull/664). This note is about why the first version went and what made the second one worth having.

## Why run tests in random order at all

A suite that always runs in the same order can hide dependencies between tests. Scenario B passes because scenario A happened to leave a row in the database, or a file on disk, or a logged-in session. Nothing in either scenario says so. You find out the day someone runs B on its own, or the day the order changes for an unrelated reason.

Gauge has always said execution order isn't guaranteed unless you ask for `--sort`. In practice, specs ran in the order they were found, and scenarios ran in the order they were written. That makes the order a consequence of the implementation, not a promise, and people come to rely on consequences. Shuffling the order on purpose is the cheapest way to find out whether a suite has that kind of hidden coupling.

## The first attempt, and why I removed it

In May 2017 we [proposed](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/issues/641) an `--order` flag with two values, `sort` and `random`, to replace the existing `--sort`. It made it into nightly builds but never into a release. On 1 June 2017, a few weeks after the proposal, I removed it again.

The reasons I gave at the time were mostly about confusion. There were now two flags that touched ordering. It wasn't clear what `--order=sort` meant when specs were split across parallel streams. And there was a philosophical worry that a built-in ordering option would encourage people to write specs that depend on each other.

Looking back, the real gap was a different one, and it took a later discussion to make it obvious.

## What random order needs

In October 2025 a contributor [asked for random order again](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/issues/2793), for the reason above: to expose hidden dependencies in an API test suite. My first reply was a list of objections, and the main one was this: if a run fails because of the order, how do you debug it? The next run will choose a different order and probably pass. You can't tell an ordering bug from ordinary flakiness, and you can't reproduce either.

Chad Wilson, another maintainer, pointed out that this is a solved problem. Tools that shuffle tests print the seed they used, and accept a seed as input, so that any run can be replayed exactly. JUnit and the Gradle test-partitioning plugins work like this. As Chad put it, you shouldn't implement random ordering without doing this.

He was right, and it changes the trade-off completely. A random order you can't replay is noise. A random order you can replay is a search: each run tries a new arrangement, and when one fails you have its address.

## What I built

The change is small. Most of it is flags and tests.

- `--sort` now takes a value: `alpha` or `random`. A bare `--sort` still means alphabetical, so existing scripts keep working.
- With `random`, Gauge seeds a pseudo-random generator, shuffles the specs, and then shuffles the scenarios within each spec. Table-driven scenarios are shuffled too, because the shuffle runs after tables have been expanded into scenarios.
- The seed is always printed. If you don't pass one, Gauge generates one from the clock and prints that.
- `--random-seed=<n>` replays a specific order.

The part that took the most thought was making `--repeat` and `--failed` work. Gauge already saves the arguments of the last run in `.gauge/lastRunCmd.json`, so that `gauge run --repeat` can rerun it. If the seed were generated inside the run, it would be lost, and `--repeat` would shuffle again. So the seed is generated before the arguments are saved, and added to them as an explicit `--random-seed`. A repeated run is then just a run with a seed, and nothing else needs to know about randomness.

## What a seed does and doesn't promise

A seed reproduces an order only for the same input. Gauge shuffles the list of specs it was given, so the same seed over the same specs gives the same order. Add a spec, remove one, or rerun only the failed ones, and the same seed still gives a deterministic order, but a different one.

For `--failed` that's the behaviour you want: you rerun a smaller set, in a fixed order, and can rerun it again. But it's worth saying plainly, because "uses the same seed" is easy to read as "uses the same order".

There's a second, smaller gap. The seed is printed in the console output and saved with the last run, but it doesn't appear in the HTML, JSON or XML reports. The contributor who asked for the feature raised this straight away. Chad's answer was that the seed on its own isn't enough to reproduce a run: you also need the other arguments, and those don't reach the report plugins today. That's still open.

## What I'd check in any runner

- **Randomness in a tool needs an address.** Any time a tool makes a random choice that affects the result, print what it used and accept it back as input. Otherwise it's adding noise to the thing people are trying to debug.
- **Save the generated value, not the instruction to generate one.** "Shuffle" isn't reproducible. "Shuffle with 1761802692487777000" is.
- **Revisit removals when the objection changes.** I removed `--order` in 2017 for reasons that were partly about naming and partly about not knowing how to make a failure reproducible. With the second problem solved, the first was a matter of choosing flag values carefully.
- **Keep the old meaning of a flag.** Turning `--sort` from a boolean into a value without breaking a bare `--sort` cost one line of flag configuration and saved every existing CI script.

The feature itself is a few dozen lines. Most of the value came from the discussion that went before it, and from someone pointing out that the problem I was worried about already had a standard answer.

---

# Spot instances and the query that must not die

By Srikanth Venugopalan, 5 October 2025. Topics: distributed, cloud.
Canonical: https://sriv.github.io/notes/spot-instances-and-the-query-that-must-not-die/

> Spot capacity is the cheapest compute a cloud will sell you, and it comes with a short warning before it's taken back. Deciding where in the stack to absorb that warning was the interesting part.

By the second half of 2025 spot instances were one of the bigger levers we had on cost: spare cloud capacity sold at a deep discount, on the understanding that the provider can take it back. AWS gives you a two-minute warning, sometimes earlier with a rebalance recommendation. Azure and GCP give you about thirty seconds. Then the machine is gone.
