By Srikanth Venugopalan, 14 May 2020. Topics: gauge, testing, concurrency.
Canonical: https://sriv.github.io/notes/gauge-suite-hooks-under-parallelism/

> Gauge's BeforeSuite hook ran once per parallel stream, not once per run. The fix was a few hundred lines. The decision behind it was that every language runner had to support threads.

Gauge, the test automation tool I worked on for several years, has a hook called `BeforeSuite`. You put things in it that should happen once: start a browser grid, seed a database, open a connection pool. Its partner, `AfterSuite`, tears them down.

In September 2019 someone filed [an issue against the Java runner](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge-java/issues/297) that was short and completely correct: when you run specs in parallel, `@BeforeSuite` and `@AfterSuite` run once for each parallel stream. Run with four streams and your database gets seeded four times, torn down four times, and probably raced in between.

## Why it happened

Gauge's core is a Go binary. The step implementations live in a separate process, a *language runner*, one per language: Java, C#, JavaScript, Python, Ruby. The core parses specs, decides what to run, and sends the runner messages like "execution starting", "run this step", "execution ending". The runner's job on "execution starting" is to call your `BeforeSuite` methods.

The original parallel execution was the simplest thing that works. Split the specs into N groups, start N runner processes, and drive each one as if it were a serial run. Each runner received its own "execution starting", so each one ran the suite hooks. From the runner's point of view it was doing exactly what it was told. "Once per suite" had quietly meant "once per process", and parallelism had made those two different things.

You can't fix that inside a runner. Four processes don't know about each other, and making them coordinate (a lock file, a leader election, a shared flag in some external store) would move a test tool's problem onto the user's machine in a fragile way.

## The threads were already there

The way out had been built years earlier for a different reason. In 2016 a user [reported Gauge crashing](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/issues/492) at 50 parallel streams: 50 JVMs on a two-core box ran out of native threads before any test started. Process-per-stream gets expensive fast when every process is a full JVM.

The answer then was a multithreaded mode. The core starts one runner and tells it how many streams to use, and the runner runs streams on threads inside one process. I wrote the first cut of that in the Java runner in September 2016, and Kashish and Apoorva did the work in the core to drive it. It shipped behind a setting, `enable_multithreading`, and for years it was the option you reached for when process-per-stream got too heavy.

Once there's a single runner process, "once per suite" has an obvious home again. That's what [the change in May 2020](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/pull/1644) did. When the runner talks to the core over gRPC and says it supports multithreading, the core now:

1. starts one runner and initialises the suite's data store once,
2. sends "execution starting" once, so `BeforeSuite` runs once,
3. starts each stream as a goroutine that sends its specs to that same runner, tagged with a stream number,
4. waits for every stream to finish,
5. sends "execution ending" once, so `AfterSuite` runs once, then stops the runner.

Getting `AfterSuite` into the right place took a second attempt; the order is the whole point, so I added tests that check the order hooks fire in, because that's the property users actually depend on. The same pull request also stopped the core starting a runner for validation and then another for execution, and started the runners for the remaining streams up front instead of lazily. The Java side was [a matching change](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge-java/pull/442) in the runner.

## The decision, not the diff

The part I'd point to is in the description of that pull request, because it isn't code. A runner that doesn't support multithreading still gets one process per stream, and in that mode each process still runs the suite hooks. I couldn't fix that without the coordination machinery I didn't want. So the honest position was:

> This brings us to the decision that all runners should support multithreading/multitasking in order to get the Suite Hooks to run as expected.

That's a statement about the plugin contract, not about one runner. It meant the Java, C# and other runners had real work to do: shared state between streams had to become thread-safe, anything stored at suite level was now shared by every stream, and any step code that assumed it owned the process was now wrong. Some of that work landed in users' own step implementations, which is the uncomfortable part. A hook that used to run in isolation now runs once while other streams wait on it.

The alternative was to keep pretending process-per-stream gave you suite semantics. It didn't, and the bug report proved users had noticed.

## What "once" should mean

- **Name the unit a hook is scoped to.** "Suite" sounded unambiguous until parallelism split one suite across processes. If a hook is "once per X", X has to be something the system can actually see.
- **Lifecycle belongs to whoever sees the whole run.** The core saw every stream; no runner did. Moving "start" and "end" to the core, and making runners pure executors in between, fixed the semantics without any cross-process coordination.
- **Some fixes are contract changes.** The code fixed the threaded path. The pull request description is what told every runner maintainer, and every user writing hooks, what was now expected of them. Writing that down plainly mattered as much as the diff.

---

# Killing plugins politely: from a fixed timeout to keep-alives

By Srikanth Venugopalan, 18 January 2019. Topics: gauge, protocols, design.
Canonical: https://sriv.github.io/notes/gauge-killing-plugins-politely/

> Gauge gave every plugin four seconds to exit after a run, then killed it. On large projects that meant killing the HTML report halfway through writing it. The fix was to let the plugin say it was still working, and it came with a limit I'd point out more loudly today.

When a Gauge run finished, the core told each plugin to shut down, waited, and then killed any plugin that hadn't exited. The wait was a setting, `plugin_kill_timeout`, and its default was 4 seconds.

Four seconds is plenty for a plugin that's idle. It isn't enough for one that's busy. The HTML report did most of its work after the run: it received the full result at the end, and then had to render every spec page, copy assets and build a search index. On a large project that took longer than four seconds, so Gauge killed it while it was writing, and the user got a half-written report or none at all. There were reports of this going back to January 2017, [here](https://github.com/getgauge/html-report/issues/120), [here](https://github.com/getgauge/html-report/issues/121) and [here](https://github.com/getgauge/html-report/issues/153).

The workaround was to raise the timeout. That works, but it means every user with a big project has to discover the setting, and every user with a hung plugin waits longer for nothing.

## The issue that framed it

In September 2018 a user [opened an issue](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/issues/1176) with a better framing than any of us had written down. Gauge kills the plugin after a fixed number of seconds, "regardless of if the plugin is actively doing work". It should instead find out whether the plugin is still doing work, and only kill it if it isn't. They suggested one way to tell: look at the timestamps of the plugin's log files.

That's the right question. A fixed timeout tries to tell a slow plugin from a stuck one by how long it takes, and that can't work, because a slow plugin on a big project and a stuck one look identical for the first four seconds, and for the first forty.

## Let the plugin say so

Log-file timestamps are a side channel. They depend on the plugin logging regularly, on where its logs go, and on file-system timestamp granularity. The plugin already had a direct channel to Gauge, though: the socket it received messages on. The plugin is also the only party that actually knows whether it's working.

So I added a message going the other way. In [gauge-proto](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge-proto/commit/a9746e1) it's called `KeepAlive`, and it carries one field, the plugin's ID. Then:

- **Gauge** ([gauge#1309](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/pull/1309), opened 18 January 2019) listens for `KeepAlive` on each plugin's connection. When it's time to shut down, it starts a kill timer for each plugin, as before. Every `KeepAlive` from that plugin resets its timer. If the timer runs out, the plugin is killed. Gauge also passes the configured `plugin_kill_timeout` to the plugin in its environment, so the plugin knows how often it needs to report in.
- **The HTML report** ([html-report#210](https://github.com/getgauge/html-report/pull/210)) starts a background ping as soon as it receives the suite result. It sends a `KeepAlive` every half of the kill timeout, never more often than every two seconds, framed the same way as every other message on that socket: a varint length followed by the protobuf bytes. When report generation finishes, it stops pinging and exits.

The effect is that the timeout stops meaning "how long a plugin may take" and starts meaning "how long a plugin may go without saying anything". A plugin doing an hour of work can take an hour, and a plugin that goes silent is still killed after four seconds. No user needs to tune anything for the common case.

It's backward compatible in both directions. A plugin that never sends `KeepAlive` gets exactly the old behaviour. A newer plugin talking to an older Gauge sends messages nobody reads, which is harmless.

## Small things the change had to get right

Two details took more care than the idea did.

**The timer is per plugin, and it only exists during shutdown.** Pings that arrive while the run is still going have no timer to reset, and Gauge ignores them. That's fine, because nothing is trying to kill the plugin then. But it means the plugin can't "bank" liveness early. It has to keep pinging until it's done.

**A timer that can be reset has to be cleaned up carefully.** The old code waited on `time.After`, a fresh timer nobody else could touch. The new one is a single `time.Timer` per plugin that two goroutines care about: the shutdown path waits on it, and the keep-alive handler resets it. When the plugin exits first, the shutdown path stops the timer, and if `Stop` says it had already fired, drains its channel, so no expiry is left sitting there. It's three lines, and the kind of three lines that are easy to leave out.

## The limit: alive is not the same as making progress

Here's what I'd say more loudly today than I did then. The HTML report's ping ran on its own goroutine, on a ticker. It proved the process was alive and that its scheduler was running. It did not prove that report generation was getting anywhere. If the report generator had hung inside its own work loop, the ping would have kept going, and Gauge would have waited forever for a plugin that would never finish. Before the change, a stuck plugin cost four seconds. After it, a plugin stuck in the wrong way could hang the end of a CI job until the job's own timeout killed everything.

The stronger version ties the ping to progress. The renderer reports "page 412 of 3,000 done", or at least only sends a heartbeat from inside its work loop, so the ping stops when the work stops. Alongside it you'd want an upper bound that no amount of pinging can extend. We had neither. In practice the HTML report didn't deadlock, so it didn't come up, but "it didn't come up" is not a design.

There's also a smaller edge. Because the ping interval has a floor of two seconds, a user who set `plugin_kill_timeout` below two seconds would see the plugin killed between pings. That's an odd setting to choose, but the code accepted it.

## The pattern

Strip away the specifics and it's the general problem of deciding when another process has failed. The supervisor can't see inside the worker. Elapsed time is the only thing it measures directly, and elapsed time can't tell a slow worker from a stuck one. Every reasonable answer moves the evidence to the party that has it. The worker sends heartbeats, a lease it renews, or progress reports, and the supervisor only judges silence.

What I'd take from Gauge's small version of it:

- **A fixed timeout is a guess about the workload.** It's wrong for the big projects, and the big projects are the ones that matter.
- **Put the evidence where the knowledge is.** The plugin knows if it's working. Ask it, over the channel you already have, not through log files.
- **Make silence the failure, not duration.** Reset on every heartbeat, and keep the timeout short.
- **A heartbeat from a separate thread proves liveness, not progress.** If a hang is a failure you care about, the heartbeat has to come from the work itself, and there has to be a ceiling it can't extend.
- **Make it optional for the other side.** A worker that never heartbeats should get the old behaviour, not a new failure.

---

# Your protocol's worst message is the summary

By Srikanth Venugopalan, 20 November 2018. Topics: gauge, protocols, design.
Canonical: https://sriv.github.io/notes/gauge-the-worst-message-is-the-summary/

> Gauge sent its report plugins one message with the entire run in it. On a big enough suite, protobuf refused to encode it. The fix was to cut the result at a boundary the format already had, and to let each plugin opt in.

In November 2018 a user [reported](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/issues/1239) that Gauge crashed before generating reports on big test runs. The HTML report plugin's log had the line that explained it:

```
Unable to connect to plugin Html Report 4.0.2. proto: message encodes to over 2 GB
fatal error: runtime: out of memory
```

Nothing was wrong with the tests. The run had finished. What failed was the last step: telling the report plugins what happened.

## One message with everything in it

Gauge's core ran specs and talked to plugins over a socket using protobuf messages. Most of those messages were small and frequent: a spec started, a scenario finished. At the very end of a run, Gauge sent each reporting plugin one more message, `SuiteExecutionResult`, holding the complete result of the run: every spec, every scenario, every step, every hook, every captured message, every screenshot. The HTML, XML and JSON reports were all built from it.

It was a natural design. A report is a view of the whole run, so give the reporter the whole run. It's also the one message whose size grows with everything: the number of specs, the length of each, how much each step logs, and how many screenshots it took. Every other message in the protocol was bounded by one event. This one was bounded by nothing.

Protobuf has a hard ceiling of 2 GB on a single encoded message. Long before you reach it, you pay for it twice: the sender holds the entire structure plus its encoded bytes in memory, and the receiver does the same in reverse. In my [comment on the issue](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/issues/1239#issuecomment-436520941) I put it this way: Gauge can't assume that much memory is available, so the fix is to send the result in chunks rather than move one giant `ProtoSuiteExecutionResult` across at the end.

## Cut where the format already has seams

The question was where to cut. Splitting the encoded bytes into arbitrary pieces would have fixed the transport and nothing else. Both sides would still need the whole thing in memory to encode and decode it, and every plugin would need new reassembly code.

The result already had natural seams. A suite result is a list of spec results. A spec is a list of items: scenarios, steps, comments, tables, tags, in document order. An item is the unit a report renders. So the change, in [gauge-proto](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge-proto/pull/17) and [Gauge](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/pull/1250), was:

1. Strip the items out of every spec result, and record on each spec how many items it had.
2. Send `SuiteExecutionResult` as before, now a skeleton: the suite totals, the spec headers, and two new fields, `chunked = true` and `chunkSize`, the number of item messages to expect.
3. Send each item as its own message, a new `SuiteExecutionResultItem`. Each item carries a new `fileName` field so the plugin can tell which spec it belongs to.

[Diagram: Before: Gauge sends the report plugin one suite result message holding every spec, step and log, which grows with the suite until protobuf refuses it at 2 GB. After: Gauge sends a skeleton marked as chunked with the item count, followed by one message per item, each carrying its spec file name so the plugin can reassemble the result. Only plugins that declare the stream_result capability receive the chunked shape.]

*Same result, cut at the item boundary the format already had.*

On the other side, the HTML report [collected the items](https://github.com/getgauge/html-report/pull/206) against their specs and built the report once it had received `chunkSize` of them. Apart from the skeleton, each message was now the size of one item rather than the size of the run. Encoding and decoding no longer needed one huge contiguous buffer on either side.

## Who gets the new shape

Gauge had more report plugins than the ones we maintained. Any plugin that received the skeleton without knowing about chunking would see specs with no items, and produce an empty report without any error. That's worse than a crash.

So chunking was opt-in. A plugin declares in its `plugin.json` that it has the `stream_result` capability. When Gauge notifies plugins, it checks each one: a plugin without the capability gets the old single message, as large as it ever was, and a plugin with it gets the skeleton followed by the items. Old plugins kept working exactly as before, including failing on huge runs exactly as before, and new ones could adopt the new shape on their own schedule.

The capability list outlived this change. When the plugin protocol later moved to gRPC, a plugin declared that it could speak it the same way, with `grpc_support`. Once a plugin can say what it understands, the core can add new behaviour without a flag day across every repository.

## What it didn't fix

Chunking fixed the protocol. It did not make the report cheap to build. The HTML plugin still accumulated every item in memory before it rendered anything, because the report it produced, with its suite-wide summary and search index, needs the whole run. A truly streaming report would have rendered each spec's page as its items arrived and kept only totals for the summary. We didn't do that. The 2 GB ceiling went away, but memory still grew with the run.

The problem also came back. In November 2022 a user with about 3,000 scenarios [hit a failure](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/issues/2305) building the HTML report. By then the plugin protocol ran on gRPC, and the report plugin capped incoming messages at 1 GB. This run sent one of 1.72 GB. There were no screenshots in it. It was response bodies the tests had logged. The [fix that time](https://github.com/getgauge/html-report/pull/291) was a setting, `gauge_max_message_size`, that raises the cap. It unblocked the user, but it's a knob, not a design. Whatever got that large still travelled as a single message.

## The general version

I've since run into the same shape in very different systems. A protocol that is otherwise made of small, bounded, per-event messages has one message that summarises everything, and that message works fine until the day the thing it summarises gets big. It's usually the summary at the end: the final result, the full snapshot, the "here's the state of the world" response to a reconnect.

What I'd take from it:

- **Look for the one message whose size isn't bounded by an event.** Go through the protocol's messages and ask what each one's size grows with. The one that grows with the history or the whole dataset is the one that will fail, and it will fail at the end, after all the work is done.
- **Cut at the seams the data already has.** Splitting bytes fixes the transport limit and nothing else. Splitting at the structure's own units, here spec items, means each piece is meaningful, each side can process pieces independently, and the receiver can actually stream if it chooses to.
- **Send the count up front.** The skeleton told the plugin how many items to expect, so the plugin knew when it was done without a separate end marker, and could tell if something went missing.
- **Let the receiver opt in.** A silent wrong answer, an empty report, is worse than a loud failure. A capability declaration lets old receivers keep the old behaviour and new ones take the new shape.
- **Raising a limit is not a fix.** It is sometimes the right thing to ship on the day, but write down that the real problem is still there.

---

# Shipping a risky language feature behind a flag, and what the flag cost

By Srikanth Venugopalan, 28 September 2018. Topics: gauge, open-source, design.
Canonical: https://sriv.github.io/notes/gauge-a-risky-feature-behind-a-flag/

> Table-driven scenarios went into Gauge behind an experimental flag in 2018. The flag did its job: it let the core ship while everything around it caught up. It also stayed for seven years, and that part was not the plan.

Gauge specs are Markdown. A spec can carry a data table, and since 2017 Gauge could run a whole spec once per row of that table, thanks to [work](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/pull/600) by a teammate that also taught it to [run those rows in parallel](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/pull/630). What people kept asking for was the same thing one level down: a table attached to a single scenario, so one scenario could iterate over its own rows without dragging the rest of the spec along. The [request](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/issues/111) was opened in March 2015. In 2017 a user called it one of the main things stopping them from moving off Cucumber.

On 28 September 2018 I opened [the pull request](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/pull/1202) that added it. Its description starts with a note I added during review: the feature is experimental, disabled by default, and enabled by setting `allow_scenario_datatable=true`. This note is about why it shipped that way, and what that choice cost later.

## Why this one was risky

Most features in a test runner are additive. A new command, a new flag on an existing command, a new report column. You can add them without changing what an existing spec means.

A scenario table is different, because it changes the language. Before the change, a table inside a scenario was just a table: a step argument, or text. After it, the same Markdown could mean "run this scenario once per row". Steps could now use dynamic parameters like `<word>` that resolve against the scenario's table, the spec's table, or both. That is a change in parsing, in resolution, and in execution, all at once. The diff touched the parser, argument lookup, the spec and scenario executors, the parallel execution path, and the protobuf messages every plugin consumed.

And Gauge was not one binary. The core ran specs, but language runners for Java, C#, Python, Ruby and JavaScript executed the steps, and separate plugins built the HTML, XML and JSON reports. The IDE plugins parsed specs themselves. A language change in the core is only finished when every one of those understands it, and they were separate repositories with their own release cycles.

The pull request's to-do list was honest about this. Execution worked: steps resolved their parameters from the scenario table, a scenario ran once per row, and a scenario that didn't use the table ran once. But the suite result didn't carry the per-row results properly yet, the HTML report didn't know about any of it, and every row's scenario result held its own copy of the whole table, which I flagged as wasteful and in need of a backward-compatible fix.

## What the flag was for

There were two other options. One was to hold the change until the core, the reports and the IDE plugins were all ready, and release them together. In an open-source project with a few maintainers and many repositories, that means the branch rots while you wait. The other was to turn it on for everyone and fix the reports as complaints arrived. Since the feature changes what existing Markdown means, that risked changing the behaviour of specs people had already written.

The flag gave a third path. The parser only treats a table under a scenario as a scenario table when the flag is set. With the flag off, nothing about an existing spec changes. With it on, people who wanted the feature badly enough could use it, knowing the console output was right and the HTML report was not. It merged on 16 October 2018 and shipped in Gauge 1.0.3.

That part worked as intended. People found it, turned it on, and told us what broke.

## What the flag didn't protect against

The first thing that broke was me. A user asked whether a scenario could load its table from an external CSV file, the way a spec could. I [said yes](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/pull/1202#issuecomment-443392044). A few weeks later someone tried it, got a parse error, and I had to [correct myself](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/pull/1202#issuecomment-449906270): it only worked with inline tables. Later that day I [admitted](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/pull/1202#issuecomment-449913828) the feature was too rough to recommend yet, mostly because the reports didn't support it. External tables at scenario level were [logged separately](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/issues/1569) and never got done. The lesson I took was small but real: when a feature is half-finished, you can't answer questions about it from what you meant to build. Answer from what's in the code.

The second was a crash, and it was not behind the flag at all. In November 2019 a user running `gauge run --parallel --only <tags>` got a [nil-pointer panic in the HTML report](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/issues/1529). The cause was in code I'd written for the feature. When parallel runs produce partial results for the same spec, Gauge merges them, and my merge marked the merged spec as table-driven unconditionally. The report plugin believed that, went looking for table rows that didn't exist, and crashed. [The fix](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/pull/1530) was a few lines: mark it table-driven only if one of the inputs was.

That bug is the useful one. A flag protects you from new behaviour leaking into old specs. It doesn't protect the code paths you had to change on the way, and you change a lot of them for a language feature. The merge path was shared between flagged and unflagged runs, so a mistake in it reached everyone.

## The cost: seven years

Then the flag simply stayed. The core was usable, so the pressure to finish went away. The parts left to do were the unglamorous ones, in other repositories. Each year a few issues arrived: [the flag not working](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/issues/1565) because of the external-table limit, results [summed up wrong](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/issues/1802) for some spec shapes, and in 2024 the copy-per-row design I'd flagged in 2018 coming back as [a memory problem](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/issues/2528) for large tables.

An experimental flag is a promise that the feature will either graduate or be removed. Nobody owned that promise, me included, and a promise nobody owns is not kept.

It was kept in the end because a contributor opened [an issue](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/issues/2790) in October 2025 with the goal stated plainly: remove the flag and make the feature the default. They'd worked out the current state, listed what was broken, and asked the right design questions, such as whether scenario tables should be allowed inside table-driven specs at all. Another user answered that they relied on exactly that combination for test matrices, so it stayed.

That gave me a reason to come back. In [one pull request](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/pull/2791) I fixed the scenario counts, the parameter validation and the JSON reporter, and deleted `allow_scenario_datatable`. That was 27 October 2025, seven years and a month after the flag went in. The same contributor then did the larger part of the remaining work: making the results sent to the report plugins say whether a scenario was driven by the spec table, the scenario table or both, with the [row it came from](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/pull/2798).

For the memory problem I [took a different approach](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/pull/2792): instead of creating every row's scenario up front, create each one when it's about to run. In the pull request's micro-benchmark, setting up a 1,000-row table went from about 9,000 allocations to 3. Most of that saving is deferred work, not removed work, because each scenario is still built when it runs. But it's only built when it's needed, and it can be dropped once it's done. That pull request is still open, and it adds a flag too: `scenario_init_strategy`, defaulting to `eager`. I noticed the irony. This time the flag exists to keep the old behaviour while people try the new one, and the exit condition is written into the PR: if the feedback is good, lazy becomes the default.

## What I'd keep and change

I'd use the flag again. For a change to what a language means, in a project spread across many repositories, it was the right tool. It let the core ship, it kept existing specs safe, and it put the feature in front of the people who wanted it.

What I'd change is everything around it:

- **Give the flag an exit condition when you add it.** "Experimental until the HTML report and the IDE plugins support it" is a list you can check. "Experimental" on its own never ends.
- **Treat shared code paths as unflagged.** Anything the flagged feature changed that the unflagged path also runs needs the same care as a normal release. The 2019 panic came from exactly there.
- **Write the known debt into the code, not only the pull request.** The copy-per-row note was in a 2018 PR description. It came back as a bug in 2024, and nobody reading the code would have seen it coming.
- **Answer from the code.** Especially about a half-finished feature you wrote yourself.

The feature is finished now, and it's default behaviour. It got there because someone outside the original team cared enough to write down what "done" meant. That's a good outcome, but not a good process to depend on.

---

# Deprecate, don't delete: the price of backward compatibility

By Srikanth Venugopalan, 21 March 2018. Topics: gauge, protocols, compatibility.
Canonical: https://sriv.github.io/notes/gauge-deprecate-dont-delete/

> Gauge's plugins were written in half a dozen languages, and all of them shared one set of protocol buffer definitions. A small rename taught me that a shared schema has more than one kind of compatibility. The rule I set afterwards still holds, and eight years on, so does its bill.

Gauge is a small core with a lot of plugins. The language runners execute steps in Java, C#, Ruby, Python, JavaScript and Go. Reporters such as the HTML report turn results into something people read. The editor integrations sit on top. They're separate repositories, released on separate schedules, and often maintained by different people. Each one talks to the core over messages defined in one shared repository, [gauge-proto](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge-proto), which every plugin pulls in and compiles into its own language.

That shared repository is a contract, and in early 2018 I learned that it has more than one side.

## A rename that looked free

In December 2017 the team added fields to carry messages written from hooks onto the report: `preHookMessage` and `postHookMessage` on specs, scenarios and suite results. A few days later they were renamed to the plural, `preHookMessages` and `postHookMessages`, because they're repeated fields. The [rename](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge-proto/commit/26968b9e) kept the field numbers.

On the wire, that's free. Protocol buffers identify a field by its number, not its name. An old runner sending field 8 and a new reporter reading field 8 agree, whatever each of them calls it, so nothing in a running installation breaks.

But wire format isn't the only contract. Every plugin compiles the definitions into code, and the names become the generated names: `getPreHookMessage()` in Java, `PreHookMessage` in Go, the corresponding property in C#. The next time any plugin updated its copy of gauge-proto, code that used the old name stopped compiling, in whichever language that plugin was written in. With protocol buffers there are at least three kinds of compatibility, and a change can keep one and break another:

| What's shared | Identified by | A rename |
|---|---|---|
| The binary wire format | field numbers | keeps it |
| The generated code in each language | field names | breaks it |
| JSON or text renderings of a message | field names | breaks it |

Even the generated-code row splits in two. A consumer that recompiles against the new definitions needs source compatibility. One that ships already compiled, like a plugin binary someone installed last year, needs binary compatibility, because it was built against the exact names and signatures of the old code. A change can keep the first and break the second.

In a single repository you'd rename, fix every call site, and move on. With plugins in six languages in separate repositories, there's no single change that fixes all the call sites. Each plugin finds out on its own, at whatever point it next updates the shared definitions.

## The rule

At the time I was chasing a set of bugs in which messages written from tests weren't showing up in the HTML report, across more than one plugin ([gauge#970](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/issues/970), [html-report#111](https://github.com/getgauge/html-report/issues/111), [gauge-csharp#117](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge-csharp/issues/117)). On 21 March 2018, while working through them, I opened [gauge-proto#11](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge-proto/pull/11), titled "deprecate instead of removing message fields".

It brought the old names back, as new fields marked deprecated, next to the new ones:

```protobuf
/// [DEPRECATED, use preHookMessages] Additional information at pre hook exec time
repeated string preHookMessage = 10 [deprecated=true];
```

That way any plugin built against either version of the definitions compiled, and the deprecation showed up as a warning instead of a broken build. A field keeps its meaning for good. A replacement is a new field with a new number. The old one is marked deprecated, documented as such, and stays until nobody reads it.

The rule I'd write down for anyone sharing protocol buffer definitions across repositories:

1. **Never change what a field number means.** Not its type, and not its meaning.
2. **Never reuse a number.** If a field really goes away, reserve its number and its name so nobody can bring them back with a different meaning.
3. **Don't rename.** To a consumer in another repository, a rename is a removal plus an addition.
4. **Replace by adding.** New field, new number, old one marked deprecated, with a note saying what to use instead.
5. **Remove last, and on purpose.** Only once you know nothing still reads the old field, and in a release that says so.

## Seven years later

In July 2025 a user asked for timestamps in RFC 3339 format ([gauge#2764](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/issues/2764)), because the human-readable format Gauge used couldn't tell apart runs that were close together. Changing the existing `timestamp` field's format would have been the smallest diff. It would also have silently broken every reporter that parses the old format, and nothing in the schema would have told them.

So [gauge-proto#111](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge-proto/pull/111) followed the same rule: `timestamp` marked deprecated, and a new `timestampISO` field added next to it on suite, spec, scenario and step results. Old reporters keep reading what they understand, and new ones can switch when they're ready.

The rule doesn't mean nothing ever breaks. In early 2024 I bumped Gauge's minor version in [#2457](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/pull/2457), and titled the change for exactly what it was: it breaks backward compatibility with plugins. When a break is unavoidable, the version number should say it, and the title should say it too, so that nobody has to work it out from a bug report.

## What compatibility costs

The rule made breaking changes rare. It didn't make compatibility free. It moved the cost, and it's worth being honest about where it went.

**Keeping compatibility, the producer pays, slowly and for good.** Today gauge-proto still marks 22 fields as deprecated in its main spec definitions, and another ten in the language server's. The hook-message fields I brought back in 2018 are still there. So are a dozen fields that carried screenshots as raw bytes inside result messages, deprecated in 2019 when screenshots moved to files on disk, which, given what [oversized result messages](https://sriv.github.io/notes/gauge-the-worst-message-is-the-summary/) had already done to us, was the right call. Each of them is something every new plugin author has to read past and work out whether to ignore. And each carries a question nobody can answer cheaply: is anything still reading it? Without a reliable picture of which plugin versions are still out there, the honest answer is "we don't know", and so the field stays.

**Breaking compatibility, the consumers pay, all at once.** Every downstream maintainer finds out on their own, at a moment they didn't choose, usually from a user's bug report. In an open-source ecosystem many of those maintainers are volunteers, and some of them have moved on. A break that costs the core team an afternoon can cost a plugin its users.

**And there's a cost that never shows up in the schema: the designs you don't get to choose.** Jon Skeet wrote about exactly this in 2015, while working on the C# code generator for protocol buffers, in ["Backwards compatibility is (still) hard"](https://codeblog.jonskeet.uk/2015/06/03/backwards-compatibility-is-still-hard/). He wanted each generated message to have a constructor with one optional parameter per field: much nicer to call than a builder. Then he walked through what happens when the schema evolves. Adding a field changes the constructor's signature, so code that recompiles is fine but anything already compiled breaks. Adding a field in the middle is worse: callers using positional arguments still compile, and their values silently bind to the wrong fields. The cleaner API lost to compatibility, and he ended up leaning towards a design that gave up a guarantee he wanted. That's the part of the bill people forget. Compatibility constrains not only what you can remove, but what you can build next.

None of this argues against the rule. It argues for knowing the price before you pay it, in either direction.

## The rule, as I'd write it now

**A shared schema is an API with several consumers per change.** The wire is one consumer. The generated code in every language is another. Anything that renders messages by name is a third.

**Compatibility is only as wide as the narrowest of those.** "It's binary compatible" is a true statement about one of them.

**Additive change is the cheaper kind, not the free kind.** A deprecated field costs a line of schema today and a little confusion every year after. A breaking change costs every downstream maintainer an afternoon, at a time they didn't choose. Usually the first bill is smaller. Know that you're choosing it.

**Count your consumers before you decide.** The real cost of a break depends on how many people compile against you and whether you can reach them. If you can't answer that, you can't price the break, which is the strongest argument for deprecating instead.

**Make the break obvious when you have to make one.** Say it in the version number and in the title, and don't leave it for a downstream maintainer to discover.

---

# IDE support, before and after the Language Server Protocol

By Srikanth Venugopalan, 29 November 2017. Topics: gauge, developer tools, protocols.
Canonical: https://sriv.github.io/notes/gauge-ide-support-before-and-after-lsp/

> I wrote Gauge's Visual Studio plugin in 2014, when every editor needed its own. Three years later the project moved to a language server. What moved into the server, and what still didn't fit in the protocol.

Gauge specifications are Markdown files, and the steps in them are bound to code in Java, C#, Ruby, Python or JavaScript. That makes editor support unusually important for a tool like Gauge. A spec is only pleasant to write if the editor can autocomplete steps you've already implemented, jump from a step to its code, flag a step nobody has implemented yet, and run a scenario from where you're looking at it.

For the first few years, each editor got that through its own plugin.

## One plugin per editor

I started the [Visual Studio plugin](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge-visualstudio) in October 2014. My first autocomplete commit is from 26 October. Within a couple of months it had syntax highlighting for steps, parameters and tags, go-to-definition from a step to its implementation, autocomplete for concepts and nested concepts, highlighting of unimplemented steps, and an action that generated a stub implementation for one. The plugin also hooked into Visual Studio's test runner, so specs and scenarios showed up as tests.

The design was simple. The plugin didn't parse specs itself. From the start it asked a running Gauge process. Gauge exposed an API over a socket, with messages defined in protocol buffers, and the plugin sent requests such as "give me all the steps" and turned the answers into completions. That split was the right instinct, and I'd keep it: Gauge already knew how to parse specs, so the editor shouldn't learn to do it a second time.

What the split didn't remove was everything around the request. For each feature, the Visual Studio plugin still needed:

- the code that starts a Gauge daemon for the open project, waits for it, and handles the cases where Gauge isn't installed or the daemon fails to start;
- the caching, plus file watchers to know when the cached steps had gone stale;
- the mapping from Gauge's answers to Visual Studio's own types for classifiers, completions, glyphs and test cases;
- the integration with debugging, in a way that differed between Visual Studio versions.

All of it was in C#, against Visual Studio's extension APIs. The IntelliJ plugin, which teammates maintained, did the same work in Java against IntelliJ's APIs. Every editor feature was built once per editor, in that editor's language, by whoever knew that editor. That isn't something a small team can keep up for long.

By 2016 the plugin had moved test execution onto a gRPC execution API in Gauge, and that helped. But that moved one feature to a shared API. It didn't move the rest.

## The language server

The Language Server Protocol fixed exactly that shape of problem. The editor speaks one standard protocol for completion, go-to-definition, diagnostics, formatting, symbols and code actions, and a server that understands the language answers. A thin client is enough to get a new editor most of the way.

Gauge's language server came from the team in 2017. Its first commit, in July, did autocomplete. Over the following months teammates added completion for parameters, formatting, execution, and validation errors as diagnostics. The server lived inside Gauge itself, and that mattered: the parser, the validation and the step index that the CLI used were the same ones the editor saw. A step that failed validation on the command line got the same diagnostic in the editor.

My part was in late 2017, next to the new [VS Code extension](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge-vscode). On 29 November I opened [#883](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/pull/883), which added document symbols and workspace symbols, so that you could jump to any spec or scenario by name in an editor that supports the protocol. The week before, I'd done the change that taught me the most about where the protocol ends.

## What didn't fit

VS Code wanted a test explorer for scenarios ([gauge-vscode#42](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge-vscode/issues/42)): a tree of specs and scenarios that you could run from the sidebar. The Language Server Protocol had nothing for that. It knows about documents, symbols and positions. It doesn't know what a test is, or which test belongs to which file, or what it means to run one.

So [#870](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/pull/870) added a custom request, `gauge/specs`, which returns the headings of every spec in the project. It's a small change. It's also a reminder that a standard protocol covers what all languages have in common, and a test tool's most important features are the parts that aren't common:

- Which scenarios exist, and in which spec.
- Running one of them, or a set of them, and reporting results while they run.
- Debugging a step, which means a runner in another language has to be started in debug mode and an editor has to attach to it.

Every one of those became a custom request or a feature in the editor extension. The editor-specific code didn't disappear. It got smaller and moved to the edge, and the part that changed most often, the understanding of specs, was written once, inside Gauge.

## Where the standard stops

**Put the understanding in the tool, from the start.** The 2014 plugin got this right before LSP existed: ask Gauge, don't re-parse. Everything that later moved into the language server was already behind an API. What LSP added was a standard way for every editor to ask.

**A standard protocol covers what all languages share.** For a test tool, the valuable part is running things, and the protocol had no word for it. Plan for custom requests, keep them few, and keep them in the same server, so that editors don't fall back to building their own.

**The cost of an editor plugin is the glue around each feature.** Lifecycle, caching, staleness, and mapping to the editor's types. A feature list doesn't show it, which is why one plugin per editor looked affordable until there were several.

The Visual Studio plugin is archived now, and so is the IntelliJ one. The VS Code extension and the language server carried on. I don't mind that ending for the plugin I wrote. It was the right design for 2014, and parts of it, asking Gauge rather than re-parsing, carried straight over into what replaced it.

---

# Telemetry we added, then deleted

By Srikanth Venugopalan, 5 June 2017. Topics: gauge, open source, privacy.
Canonical: https://sriv.github.io/notes/gauge-telemetry-we-added-then-deleted/

> In 2017 I wired anonymous usage telemetry into Gauge. Two years later we took it all out. Adding it took a few weeks; most of what I learned was about the parts around the ping.

Gauge was built by a small team. We didn't have the time to run user studies or surveys, and we wanted to know which commands and flags people actually used before we changed or deprecated any of them. So in May 2017 the team opened two issues: give every installation an anonymous identifier ([#653](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/issues/653)), and collect statistics on which commands get run ([#658](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/issues/658)). I picked them up, and on 5 June 2017 I opened [the pull request](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/pull/665) that introduced an install ID and sent anonymous events to Google Analytics.

The ping itself was the easy part. A UUID per installation, saved under the user's Gauge config directory. An event per command, sent over the Measurement Protocol, with the IP address anonymised. The rule in the issue was strict and it was the right rule: never record anything specific to the user's project. `gauge run myspecfolder` records that `run` happened, not the folder. `--dir="../"` records nothing about the directory. What we tracked was the language and plugins in the manifest, which execution flags were used (tags, parallel, sort, verbose), and whether refactoring was used, without its parameters.

Everything else took longer than the ping.

## Opt-in or opt-out

The first decision was the default, and I argued for opt-out: on by default, with an easy way to turn it off. The reason I gave at the time was that unattended runs would otherwise never show up. A large share of Gauge runs happened in CI, where nobody is around to answer a prompt, and an opt-in default would have told us about laptops and nothing about pipelines.

That reasoning holds up, but I'd frame the decision differently now. Opt-out isn't a technical default; it's a promise you make to every user who never reads the docs. Keeping that promise is what the rest of this note is about.

The code went in with telemetry disabled while we tested it against a separate analytics account, and the team turned it on for the 0.9.0 release in July 2017. The same day, the project published a post, [Why we collect data](https://gauge.org/2017/07/20/why-we-collect-data/). It said what was collected, where it was stored, who could see it, and how to turn it off. I still think the post mattered as much as the code.

## Human or machine

Once events were flowing, the first problem was that one CI server could run Gauge thousands of times a day, and those runs looked exactly like people. So I added a CI flag to every event ([#702](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/issues/702)). There's no single standard way to detect CI, so it was a table: `GO_SERVER_URL` for GoCD, `JENKINS_URL` for Jenkins, the TeamCity variable, and `CI=true` for Travis, AppVeyor, CircleCI and the rest. It's an unglamorous list, and it's what made the numbers mean anything: human usage and machine usage answer different questions.

## Fast commands lose their events

Testing turned up something I hadn't expected: quick commands weren't being recorded at all. `gauge uninstall`, `gauge format`, `gauge install` with no arguments. The command finished and the process exited before the HTTP request did. The fix was to make those commands wait for the telemetry request before exiting. That trades a little latency for complete data, and if I did it again I'd put a short timeout on the wait, so a slow network can't hold up someone's terminal.

It's a small bug, but it changes what you can trust. A sampling bias like that doesn't show up as an error. It shows up as "nobody uses `format`", which is exactly the kind of conclusion telemetry was supposed to make safe.

## Off has to be easy in every place Gauge runs

`gauge telemetry off` worked for someone at a terminal. It didn't work for a Docker image, a CI agent built from a script, or a corporate machine provisioned by an installer. So "off" had to exist everywhere:

- An environment variable, `GAUGE_TELEMETRY_ENABLED`, that takes priority over the config file ([#736](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/issues/736)), with a message that tells you when the variable is the thing deciding.
- A page in the Windows installer to turn it off, and a `/TELEMETRY off` switch for silent installs ([#741](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/pull/741)). Teammates added the same for the macOS and Linux installers.
- Our own CI pipelines, where we turned telemetry off, so that we weren't counting ourselves.

## Telling people, every time

A year later the team felt that opt-out needed to be more visible ([#1121](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/issues/1121)). The change was that every `gauge run` would say that telemetry was on and point at how to change it, until the user made an explicit choice. I implemented that in [#1123](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/pull/1123): Gauge now recorded whether you had actually chosen, not just the current value, and the notice went away once you had. Saying "on" counted as a choice, and so did saying "off".

That's the version I'd start with next time. The notice made opt-out much closer to informed consent, at the cost of one line of output. It's also what a user who never reads the docs actually sees.

## Taking it out

In October 2019 the team decided Gauge no longer needed to keep the data, and [#1490](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/issues/1490) listed what removing it meant:

1. the telemetry code in Gauge
2. the telemetry code in Gauge's JavaScript packaging
3. the telemetry messages
4. the telemetry configuration
5. the telemetry prompts in the VS Code extension
6. the unique ID generation
7. the documentation
8. the blog post
9. the analytics account itself

Removing it took a teammate's [pull request](https://github.com/getgauge/gauge/pull/1511) and a few weeks, and the `telemetry` command stayed behind as deprecated, so that scripts calling it wouldn't break. The blog post now opens by saying that Gauge no longer collects telemetry, which I think is the right way to leave it: anyone who reads the old explanation sees straight away that it no longer applies.

## What I'd keep

Nine items is the honest measure of what the feature cost. The ping was one of them. The rest was everything a promise to users touches: the installers, the editor extension, the config, the docs, a public post. If I add telemetry to a tool again, I'd write that removal list first, before the first event is sent. Then everyone knows what the feature costs to remove, and it's easier to keep it to what you'd be willing to explain.

The other things I'd keep:

- **Never record anything about the user's project.** Command names and flags, never paths or values.
- **Mark machine runs.** Without a CI flag, the numbers mostly describe CI.
- **Check that short commands still get counted.** Missing data is a bias, and it never shows up as an error.
- **Make off work wherever the tool runs.** Command, environment variable, installer.
- **Tell people, until they've chosen.** One line of output, until the user has picked either way.
